nezha-agent spawning credential-access shell commands on Linux (post-RCE) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the post-exploitation footprint of Nezha CVE-2026-46716 on victim hosts: the nezha-agent process (typically running as root) executes a shell child that reads /etc/shadow or curls the cloud instance-metadata endpoint — exactly the PoC payload in the advisory. Targets Linux EDR / auditd process telemetry. Rationale: Pins on the named binary `nezha-agent` (the gRPC TaskStream sink that runs `cr.Command` per `service/singleton/crontask.go:133-181`) as parent, combined with the exact recon-string set from the advisory's PoC (`cat /etc/shadow`, `curl http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/`). Nezha-agent is a passive monitoring agent — these strings under its process tree are inherently malicious. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-99gv-2m7h-3hh9 • https://github.com/nezhahq/nezha • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/nezha-abused-post-exploitation/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/005/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/008/
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1003.008 T1552.005 T1057
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin-authored Nezha cron task that genuinely greps /etc/shadow for password-aging audits (rare, validate don't suppress)
  • Cloud-onboarding script delivered via Nezha cron that queries IMDS for instance tags (validate against admin change-ticket)
  • Security team running a controlled exploit validation of CVE-2026-46716 on staging
  • Backup tooling that happens to be parented under nezha-agent on a host where Nezha invokes pre-snapshot hooks
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "audit" and AccountName in~ ("root","security-audit") and DeviceName has_any ("audit-","compliance-"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: Identify the host (DeviceName) and confirm the parent process is the legitimate nezha-agent binary (hash + path under typical install dir like /opt/nezha/agent/ or /usr/local/bin/). Inspect the full child command line — the PoC chain `id; hostname; cat /etc/shadow; curl ... iam/security-credentials` is distinctive. 2) Contain: Stop the nezha-agent service on the affected host (`systemctl stop nezha-agent`) to halt further task execution. On the dashboard, identify the cron entry whose ID matches the executed task and delete the row; revoke the offending RoleMember account and its JWT. Rotate any credentials that the IMDS query would have exposed (instance-role STS tokens, GCE service-account tokens). 3) Hunt: Enumerate ALL hosts running nezha-agent (the cron fan-outs to every server in ServerShared) and pivot UC2 across them; the exploit pushes to every agent simultaneously. Check the dashboard's notification table for member-owned webhooks and pull outbound traffic from the
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has "nezha-agent"
   or InitiatingProcessParentFileName has "nezha-agent"
| where FileName in~ ("cat","less","more","head","tail","awk","sed","grep","curl","wget","sh","bash","dash","python","python3","perl")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (
    "/etc/shadow",
    "169.254.169.254",
    "iam/security-credentials",
    "metadata.google.internal",
    "metadata.azure.com",
    "/computeMetadata/v1",
    "/latest/meta-data"
  )
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd   = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          GrandparentImage = InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
          ChildImage  = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd    = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
// Linux via ASIM (Defender for Endpoint Linux / Sysmon-Linux / auditd via ASIM parsers)
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DvcOs has "Linux" or ActingProcessName has "nezha-agent" or ParentProcessName has "nezha-agent"
| where ParentProcessName has "nezha-agent"
    or ActingProcessName has "nezha-agent"
    or ParentProcessCommandLine has "nezha-agent"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any (
    "/etc/shadow",
    "169.254.169.254",
    "iam/security-credentials",
    "metadata.google.internal",
    "metadata.azure.com",
    "/computeMetadata/v1",
    "/latest/meta-data"
  )
   or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (
    "/etc/shadow",
    "169.254.169.254",
    "iam/security-credentials"
  )
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine,
          TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Nezha Monitoring Agent Spawning Credential-Access Recon (CVE-2026-46716 Post-RCE)

status: experimental
description: Detects the nezha-agent process spawning a shell or LOLBin that touches /etc/shadow or the cloud instance-metadata service — the exact PoC payload from GHSA-99gv-2m7h-3hh9.
references:

logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: linux
detection:

    sensitive_targets:

            - '/etc/shadow'

            - 'iam/security-credentials'

nezha-agent outbound network connection to cloud instance-metadata service AIActions on Objectives High
Detects a network connection from any process under the nezha-agent process tree to the cloud instance-metadata endpoint (169.254.169.254 / metadata.google.internal / metadata.azure.com). This is the cleanest post-RCE signal for Nezha CVE-2026-46716 because nezha-agent has no legitimate reason to query IMDS — its monitoring telemetry goes to the dashboard's gRPC endpoint, not the cloud metadata API. Rationale: Targets the IMDS endpoint named verbatim in the advisory's PoC (`curl -s http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/`) and pins the source to nezha-agent's process tree. Nezha agents communicate with their dashboard over gRPC — they have zero legitimate reason to touch IMDS, making this a near-deterministic post-exploit signal. Distinct pivot from UC2 (network telemetry vs. process telemetry — catches cases where the EXECVE was missed but the connection was logged). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-99gv-2m7h-3hh9 • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/005/ • https://github.com/nezhahq/nezha
ATT&CKT1552.005 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Cloud-init or instance metadata probe triggered by an admin-authored Nezha cron that legitimately queries the local tag service (rare; validate via change-ticket rather than allow-list)
  • SSRF-protection telemetry tools tagging the nezha-agent process during a security validation
  • Misattribution where a sibling process under a shared cgroup is logged with nezha-agent context (verify the actual EXECVE chain in DeviceProcessEvents)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("cloud-init", "ec2-instance-connect") and AccountName == "root" and InitiatingProcessParentFileName has "systemd")
Response runbook
1) Triage: Confirm the connection's initiating process chain truly traces back to nezha-agent (use DeviceProcessEvents to walk the PID tree). Inspect the URL path requested — `/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/` (AWS) or `/computeMetadata/v1/instance/service-accounts/` (GCP) means an IAM token was lifted. 2) Contain: Stop nezha-agent on the host; rotate the instance-attached IAM role / service-account credentials immediately (treat as compromised). Block egress from the host to 169.254.169.254 if possible until investigation completes. On the dashboard, identify and delete the offending cron row, disable the RoleMember account, and patch to a commit after 50dc8e6. 3) Hunt: Pivot CloudTrail / GCP audit / Azure activity for any API call authenticated by the stolen STS / metadata token (filter by `userIdentity.sessionContext.sourceIdentity` for the instance role) in the 24h window after the IMDS hit. Run UC2/UC3 across every host running nezha-agent — the exploit fan-out hits all
// Two-stage: find IMDS connections, then filter to those whose initiating process chain includes nezha-agent
let ImdsHits = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where RemoteIP == "169.254.169.254"
       or RemoteUrl has_any ("169.254.169.254", "metadata.google.internal", "metadata.azure.com")
    | project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort,
              InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessFileName,
              InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
              InitiatingProcessAccountName;
ImdsHits
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has "nezha-agent"
   or InitiatingProcessParentFileName has "nezha-agent"
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "nezha-agent"
// Catch grandparent chain via process-tree lookup
| union (
    ImdsHits
    | join kind=inner (
        DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessFileName has "nezha-agent"
        | project DeviceId, ChildPid=ProcessId, ChildFile=FileName, ChildCmd=ProcessCommandLine, ChildTime=Timestamp
    ) on DeviceId
    | where InitiatingProcessId == ChildPid and Timestamp between (ChildTime .. ChildTime + 10m)
  )
| order by Timestamp desc
// Network connection to IMDS where the originating process chain involves nezha-agent
let ImdsConn = ImNetworkSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where DstIpAddr == "169.254.169.254"
       or DstHostname has_any ("metadata.google.internal", "metadata.azure.com");
let NezhaProcs = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where ActingProcessName has "nezha-agent"
       or ParentProcessName has "nezha-agent"
       or ParentProcessCommandLine has "nezha-agent"
    | project DvcHostname, NezhaProcPid=TargetProcessId, NezhaTime=TimeGenerated, NezhaCmd=TargetProcessCommandLine;
ImdsConn
| join kind=inner NezhaProcs on DvcHostname
| where TimeGenerated between (NezhaTime .. NezhaTime + 10m)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, DstPortNumber, NezhaCmd, NezhaTime
| order by TimeGenerated desc

FileBrowser Quantum public share PATCH path traversal in fromPath/toPath (GHSA-qqqm-5547-774x) AIExploitation High
Detects exploitation of the unauthenticated path traversal in FileBrowser Quantum's publicPatchHandler. Targets HTTP PATCH requests to /public/api/resources?hash=<share-hash> whose JSON body contains '..' segments in the fromPath or toPath fields — the exact pattern that escapes the share root before SanitizeUserPath runs. Rationale: Pivots on the verbatim exploit-request shape from the advisory: HTTP PATCH against /public/api/resources with hash= query string, where the JSON body contains a fromPath or toPath value beginning with '..'. Confirmed against the GitLab Advisories writeup of the sibling CVE-2026-44542 (same handler family, same root-cause sanitize-after-join pattern). Defender/Falcon left empty because EDR telemetry does not include HTTP request bodies — this is exclusively a WAF/web-proxy detection. Cross-checked: https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/gtsteffaniak/filebrowser/CVE-2026-44542/, https://github.com/gtsteffaniak/filebrowser/security/advisories/GHSA-fwj3-42wh-8673, https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-44542, https://deepwiki.com/gtsteffaniak/filebrowser/2.3-api-design. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/gtsteffaniak/filebrowser/CVE-2026-44542/ • https://github.com/gtsteffaniak/filebrowser/security/advisories/GHSA-fwj3-42wh-8673 • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-44542 • https://deepwiki.com/gtsteffaniak/filebrowser/2.3-api-design
ATT&CKT1190 T1083
Data sourcesWeb.All_Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate user renaming a file inside an AllowModify public share to a name that begins with two dots (e.g. '..hidden.txt') — the fromPath/toPath value literally contains '..' as part of the filename, not a traversal segment
  • Internal vulnerability scanners (Nuclei, Burp, nmap http-scripts) probing the endpoint after a sanctioned pen-test starts
  • QA / staging traffic that intentionally fuzzes the PATCH endpoint with traversal payloads to verify the patched version
  • Backup-and-restore tooling that writes JSON containing '..\segments' in file paths if it shares the same nginx pipeline
Suppression filter
and not (BodySource matches regex @"(?i)""(from|to)Path""\s*:\s*""\.\.[A-Za-z0-9_-]") // exclude filenames literally starting with '..' followed by a name char rather than a path separator
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull the full request body for the matched event, decode the JSON, confirm fromPath/toPath has a leading '../' (not a filename containing '..'). Check the FileBrowser version on the target host via `/api/health` or process inventory — versions before commit 28e9b81e438e (2026-05-18) are vulnerable. Identify the share owner from the hash. Step 2 — Contain: if exploitation is confirmed, immediately revoke the share (DELETE /api/shares/<hash>), rotate any credentials/secrets in files the share owner had read access to within the source root, and block the source IP at the perimeter. Upgrade FileBrowser to the fixed release. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on the source IP across 30 days for any other PATCH/PUT/DELETE against /public/api/* (sibling endpoints with same handler family), enumerate every share-hash the IP touched, and review GET requests on those hashes within ±15 minutes of the PATCH (file pulled into share, then downloaded).
let endpoint = "/public/api/resources";
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestMethod =~ "PATCH"
| where RequestURL contains endpoint
| where RequestURL contains "hash="
| extend BodySource = coalesce(tostring(DeviceCustomString1), tostring(DeviceCustomString2), tostring(DeviceCustomString3), tostring(DeviceCustomString4), tostring(DeviceCustomString5), tostring(DeviceCustomString6), tostring(RequestContext), tostring(Message))
| where BodySource matches regex @"(?i)""(from|to)Path""\s*:\s*""[^""]*\.\."
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceUserName, RequestClientApplication, RequestMethod, RequestURL, EventOutcome, BodySource, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Volumetric PATCH probing against FileBrowser Quantum public share endpoint AIReconnaissance Medium
Catches automated path-traversal probing where one source IP issues many PATCH requests with varying body shapes against /public/api/resources?hash=<hash> in a short window. Targets attacker tooling enumerating share hashes or fuzzing fromPath/toPath values for the GHSA-qqqm-5547-774x bug — distinct from a single legitimate rename operation. Rationale: A single legitimate user renaming a file via a public share generates one PATCH; an attacker fuzzing fromPath/toPath payloads or enumerating share hashes generates many in a tight window. Threshold pivots: ≥10 PATCHes from one IP in 5 min, OR ≥3 distinct hash= values from one IP in 5 min. Datadog query is the raw filter — the count/groupBy threshold is set at rule level per the Datadog Cloud SIEM model. Defender/Falcon empty because HTTP telemetry isn't on the EDR. Cross-checked: https://github.com/gtsteffaniak/filebrowser/security/advisories/GHSA-fwj3-42wh-8673, https://github.com/gtsteffaniak/filebrowser/releases. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/gtsteffaniak/filebrowser/security/advisories/GHSA-fwj3-42wh-8673 • https://github.com/gtsteffaniak/filebrowser/releases • https://deepwiki.com/gtsteffaniak/filebrowser/2.3-api-design
ATT&CKT1190 T1595.002
Data sourcesWeb.All_Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned external pen-test or red-team exercise probing the FileBrowser instance from a single source IP
  • Vulnerability scanner (Tenable, Qualys, Rapid7, Nuclei) running its CVE-2026-44542 / GHSA-qqqm-5547-774x check from a known scan node
  • Mobile FileBrowser client retrying a flaky network during a bulk-rename of many files — single hash, many PATCHes
  • Sync agent reconciling state after reconnect issues PATCHes back-to-back to the same share hash
Suppression filter
and SourceIP !in ((_GetWatchlist('AuthorizedScanners') | project SearchKey)) and RequestClientApplication !has_any ("Nessus", "Qualys", "Nuclei", "InsightVM")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: confirm the source IP is not an authorised scanner (check vulnerability-management allowlist) and that the FileBrowser instance is exposed to the internet rather than internal. Pull a sample of the PATCH bodies — if any body contains '..' in fromPath/toPath, escalate to UC1 logic immediately. Step 2 — Contain: if the source IP is unauthorised and bodies show '..' segments, block at the WAF/perimeter, revoke any share-hash the IP successfully PATCHed, and force a FileBrowser upgrade to the post-28e9b81e438e build. Step 3 — Hunt: search 30 days of WAF logs for the same source IP touching /public/api/* sibling endpoints (bulk-DELETE, PUT — same handler family). Pivot on each share-hash the IP enumerated: review the share owner's file system for files moved or renamed outside the share root.
let WindowMin = 5m;
let PatchThreshold = 10;
let HashThreshold = 3;
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestMethod =~ "PATCH"
| where RequestURL contains "/public/api/resources"
| extend ShareHash = extract(@"(?i)[?&]hash=([A-Za-z0-9_-]+)", 1, RequestURL)
| summarize PatchCount = count(),
            UniqueHashes = dcount(ShareHash),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            UserAgents = make_set(RequestClientApplication, 25),
            StatusCodes = make_set(EventOutcome, 25)
            by SourceIP, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, bin(TimeGenerated, WindowMin)
| where PatchCount >= PatchThreshold or UniqueHashes >= HashThreshold
| extend ProbeSignal = case(UniqueHashes >= HashThreshold and PatchCount >= PatchThreshold, "hash_enumeration",
                            PatchCount >= 20, "single_hash_fuzzing",
                            "elevated")
| order by PatchCount desc
source:(nginx OR caddy OR apache OR aws.waf OR cloudflare OR azure.appgw) @http.method:PATCH @http.url:*\/public\/api\/resources*

Megalodon harvester: curl POST to C2 /collect endpoint on Linux runner AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the runtime exfil step of the Megalodon payload — a curl invocation POSTing gzipped credential blob to https://216.126.225.129:8443/collect. Catches both self-hosted runners and any Linux/Windows host re-executing the decoded payload. Rationale: Pivots on the verbatim exfil command in the article — curl POST to https://216.126.225.129:8443/collect with --data-binary. Combining curl binary + IP + /collect path makes a near-zero-FP detection that catches the payload even if the decoded bash is split across multiple invocations.
ATT&CKT1567.002 T1041 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IR/red-team replaying the public payload on a test runner
  • Reverse-engineer detonating the decoded bash in a sandbox
  • Detection-engineering validation test in non-prod
  • Threat-intel scraper fetching the exact URL
Response runbook
Triage: confirm process tree — initiating bash should be child of a GitHub Actions Runner.Listener / runsvc.sh / runner-worker process for a self-hosted runner, or any sh/bash on a non-runner host. Inspect ProcessCommandLine for the full curl argv (`-X POST`, `--data-binary @-`). Contain: kill the curl PID, isolate host, block 216.126.225.129/32 egress. If a GitHub Actions runner: deregister the runner, revoke its registration token, and rotate the repo/org-level PAT and any OIDC trust relationships exposed. Hunt: same aid/DeviceName — look for preceding bash with base64 -d piping into bash, env dump, ~/.ssh/id_* reads (UC5), and grep with API_KEY/SECRET/TOKEN pattern (UC3). Cross-check GitHub for recent workflow file changes on the repo whose runner fired.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "curl" or FileName =~ "curl.exe" or FolderPath endswith "/curl"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "216.126.225.129" and ProcessCommandLine has "/collect"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName endswith "curl" or ActingProcessName endswith "curl.exe"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "216.126.225.129" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "/collect"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Megalodon harvester: bash secret-grep across workspace (API_KEY|SECRET|TOKEN|PRIVATE_KEY|BEGIN RSA) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the recursive secret-scrape step of the Megalodon payload — `grep -rE "(API_KEY|SECRET|TOKEN|PASSWORD|PRIVATE_KEY|BEGIN RSA)"` walking the CI checkout looking for hardcoded secrets. The literal token list is the article-published payload string. Rationale: All six tokens (API_KEY, SECRET, TOKEN, PASSWORD, PRIVATE_KEY, BEGIN RSA) appear verbatim in the published bash payload's grep regex. Requiring all six together discriminates Megalodon from generic secret-scanners (gitleaks/trufflehog use their own ruleset, not raw greps with this exact token list).
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1083
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Ad-hoc developer secret-audit shell one-liners
  • Custom in-house secret-scanning script using this exact pattern
  • Security training/CTF exercises using this canonical pattern
  • Pre-commit hooks running grep-based secret scans
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("gitleaks","trufflehog","detect-secrets","semgrep","ggshield") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("gitleaks","trufflehog","--baseline","pre-commit")
Response runbook
Triage: inspect parent process — is this running under a CI runner identity (e.g. `runner`, `gitlab-runner`, `dockerexec`), a service account on a build host, or an interactive user? Megalodon variant always spawns from base64-decoded bash under the runner-worker tree. Contain: if running on a CI runner, terminate the job and deregister the runner. Rotate every secret accessible to that pipeline (cloud IAM, npm tokens, GitHub PATs). Hunt: pivot on same aid/DeviceName for UC1 (egress to C2), UC2 (curl /collect), and UC5 (cred-file fan-out). Check upstream GitHub for recent workflow edits authored by build-bot@github-ci.com or ci-pipeline@actions-bot.com.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "grep" or FolderPath endswith "/grep"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_all ("API_KEY", "SECRET", "TOKEN", "PASSWORD", "PRIVATE_KEY", "BEGIN RSA")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName endswith "grep"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_all ("API_KEY", "SECRET", "TOKEN", "PASSWORD", "PRIVATE_KEY", "BEGIN RSA")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Megalodon backdoor workflow file (SysDiag.yml / Optimize-Build.yml) written to .github/workflows/ AIInstallation High
Detects creation of a workflow file with one of the two campaign-specific filenames inside any .github/workflows/ directory. Catches developer workstations that cloned/pulled a poisoned repository as well as self-hosted runners checking out the malicious tree. Rationale: Both filenames (SysDiag.yml, Optimize-Build.yml) and the `name:` field values SysDiag / Optimize-Build are called out as the two campaign variants in the article and the recommended GitHub code search anchors. The path scope (.github/workflows/) plus exact filename match make this near-zero-FP.
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1554
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate project genuinely naming a workflow SysDiag.yml or Optimize-Build.yml — exceedingly rare
  • IR/red-team adding the IOC file to a test repo for detection validation
  • Threat-intel analyst pulling the SafeDep megalodon-campaign-commits.csv reference repo locally
Response runbook
Triage: inspect the file content — confirm the workflow `name:` field is SysDiag or Optimize-Build and the run block contains a base64 blob piped to bash. Cross-reference the repo against SafeDep's megalodon-campaign-commits.csv. Contain: alert the repo owner; revert the malicious commit via `git revert <sha>`; force-pull a clean copy and require branch-protection with mandatory PR reviews on the default branch. If the workflow ever ran on a self-hosted runner, treat all secrets and OIDC trust relationships exposed to that runner as compromised. Hunt: search all org repos for the same two filenames and for commits authored by build-bot@github-ci.com / ci-pipeline@actions-bot.com with messages 'ci: add build optimization step' / 'chore: optimize pipeline runtime' / 'chore: update ci/cd pipeline'.

| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FolderPath has ".github\\workflows" or FolderPath has ".github/workflows"
| where FileName in~ ("SysDiag.yml","Optimize-Build.yml")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where TargetFilePath has ".github/workflows" or TargetFilePath has ".github\\workflows"
| where TargetFileName in~ ("SysDiag.yml","Optimize-Build.yml")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Megalodon harvester: clustered read of ~/.ssh/id_*, ~/.kube/config, ~/.npmrc, ~/.docker/config.json in one session AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the credential-collection fan-out pattern — a single process tree reading multiple distinct credential stores (SSH private key, kube config, npm token, Docker registry creds) within a one-minute window. Catches Megalodon even if the bash one-liner is split into separate cat invocations and the C2 IP is not yet contactable. Rationale: Anchors directly on the article's decoded payload (Code blocks 2 and 3) — the exact targets cat'd by the Megalodon harvester: /proc/1/environ, ~/.ssh/id_*, ~/.kube/config, ~/.npmrc, ~/.docker/config.json. Requiring ≥3 distinct targets from the same parent within 1 minute discriminates from any single legitimate dotfile-reading tool.
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1552.004 T1555
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Ansible/Chef/Puppet provisioning role enumerating user credentials
  • Container-image bake script copying user dotfiles into an image
  • Backup agent (restic, borg) walking $HOME
  • Developer running `dotfiles install` or similar bootstrap script
  • Kubernetes/cloud SDK install scripts merging multiple credential files
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("ansible-playbook","puppet","chef-client","salt-call","restic","borg","rsync") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("ansible","--inventory","site.pp","chef-solo")
Response runbook
Triage: identify parent process. Megalodon harvester runs under a child of the GitHub Actions runner-worker (Runner.Worker / runsvc.sh) or under a base64-decoded bash. A legitimate config-management tool will run as ansible/puppet/chef child of cron or sshd. Contain: if on a CI runner, terminate the job, deregister the runner, rotate all secrets in scope of the pipeline. Rotate SSH keys read; revoke npm tokens; cycle kube config service-account tokens; rotate Docker registry creds. Hunt: pivot on same DeviceName for UC1 (egress to 216.126.225.129) and UC2 (curl /collect). Look for preceding `bash -c "echo <base64> | base64 -d | bash"` invocation. Audit GitHub for matching workflow file additions in the org.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let WindowMin = 1m;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where FileName =~ "cat" or FolderPath endswith "/cat"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/proc/1/environ","/.ssh/id_","/.kube/config","/.npmrc","/.docker/config.json")
| extend Target = case(
    ProcessCommandLine has "/proc/1/environ","pid1_env",
    ProcessCommandLine has "/.ssh/id_","ssh_key",
    ProcessCommandLine has "/.kube/config","kube",
    ProcessCommandLine has "/.npmrc","npm",
    ProcessCommandLine has "/.docker/config.json","docker",
    "")
| summarize
    DistinctTargets = dcount(Target),
    Targets = make_set(Target, 10),
    SampleCmds = make_set(ProcessCommandLine, 10),
    FirstSeen = min(Timestamp),
    LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
    by DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, bin(Timestamp, WindowMin)
| where DistinctTargets >= 3
| order by LastSeen desc
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let WindowMin = 1m;
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where ActingProcessName endswith "cat"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("/proc/1/environ","/.ssh/id_","/.kube/config","/.npmrc","/.docker/config.json")
| extend Target = case(
    ActingProcessCommandLine has "/proc/1/environ","pid1_env",
    ActingProcessCommandLine has "/.ssh/id_","ssh_key",
    ActingProcessCommandLine has "/.kube/config","kube",
    ActingProcessCommandLine has "/.npmrc","npm",
    ActingProcessCommandLine has "/.docker/config.json","docker",
    "")
| summarize
    DistinctTargets = dcount(Target),
    Targets = make_set(Target, 10),
    SampleCmds = make_set(ActingProcessCommandLine, 10),
    FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
    LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
    by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, bin(TimeGenerated, WindowMin)
| where DistinctTargets >= 3
| order by LastSeen desc
source:linux.auditd @process.executable.path:*\/cat @process.command_line:(*\/proc\/1\/environ* OR *\/.ssh\/id_* OR *\/.kube\/config* OR *\/.npmrc* OR *\/.docker\/config.json*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\/cat$/i CommandLine=/(\/proc\/1\/environ|\/\.ssh\/id_|\/\.kube\/config|\/\.npmrc|\/\.docker\/config\.json)/
| case {
    CommandLine=/\/proc\/1\/environ/ | target := "pid1";
    CommandLine=/\/\.ssh\/id_/ | target := "ssh";
    CommandLine=/\/\.kube\/config/ | target := "kube";
    CommandLine=/\/\.npmrc/ | target := "npm";
    CommandLine=/\/\.docker\/config\.json/ | target := "docker";
  }
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ParentBaseFileName], function=[count(field=target, distinct=true, as=distinct_targets), collect([target])])
| distinct_targets >= 3
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmds from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=cat (Processes.process="*/proc/1/environ*" OR Processes.process="*/.ssh/id_*" OR Processes.process="*/.kube/config*" OR Processes.process="*/.npmrc*" OR Processes.process="*/.docker/config.json*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_id Processes.parent_process_name _time span=1m | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | eval is_ssh=if(match(mvjoin(cmds,"|"),"/.ssh/id_"),1,0), is_kube=if(match(mvjoin(cmds,"|"),"/.kube/config"),1,0), is_npm=if(match(mvjoin(cmds,"|"),"/.npmrc"),1,0), is_proc=if(match(mvjoin(cmds,"|"),"/proc/1/environ"),1,0), is_docker=if(match(mvjoin(cmds,"|"),"/.docker/config.json"),1,0) | eval distinct_targets=is_ssh+is_kube+is_npm+is_proc+is_docker | where distinct_targets>=3 | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmds from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=cat (Processes.process="*/proc/1/environ*" OR Processes.process="*/.ssh/id_*" OR Processes.process="*/.kube/config*" OR Processes.process="*/.npmrc*" OR Processes.process="*/.docker/config.json*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_id Processes.parent_process_name _time span=1m | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | eval is_ssh=if(match(mvjoin(cmds,"|"),"/.ssh/id_"),1,0), is_kube=if(match(mvjoin(cmds,"|"),"/.kube/config"),1,0), is_npm=if(match(mvjoin(cmds,"|"),"/.npmrc"),1,0), is_proc=if(match(mvjoin(cmds,"|"),"/proc/1/environ"),1,0), is_docker=if(match(mvjoin(cmds,"|"),"/.docker/config.json"),1,0) | eval distinct_targets=is_ssh+is_kube+is_npm+is_proc+is_docker | where distinct_targets>=3 | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("acac5a9854650c4ae2883c4740bf87d34120c038") or SHA1 in~ ("acac5a9854650c4ae2883c4740bf87d34120c038") or MD5 in~ ("acac5a9854650c4ae2883c4740bf87d34120c038")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("acac5a9854650c4ae2883c4740bf87d34120c038") or SHA1 in~ ("acac5a9854650c4ae2883c4740bf87d34120c038") or MD5 in~ ("acac5a9854650c4ae2883c4740bf87d34120c038")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["acac5a9854650c4ae2883c4740bf87d34120c038"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

YesWiki Bazar form-import volumetric POST — CVE-2026-46670 blind SQLi extraction loop AIExploitation High
Hunts the byte-by-byte extraction loop used to exploit CVE-2026-46670 in YesWiki. The PoC drives one POST to /?BazaR&vue=formulaire per character of the hex-encoded value being exfiltrated from yeswiki_users, producing dozens-to-hundreds of POSTs to a single URI from a single source IP in a short window — an unusual pattern for a wiki application. Rationale: Locks on the article's exact request shape (POST + csUriQuery containing both 'BazaR' and 'vue=formulaire') and the unavoidable property of the PoC: blind extraction requires N requests for N characters of the password hash, so a per-source-IP POST count >=20 in 5 min to this single endpoint is a strong signal that something other than a human is wiki-ing. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-jwvv-qr7q-cv8j • https://github.com/YesWiki/yeswiki/blob/1f485c049db030b94c047ec219e63534ac81142e/tools/bazar/services/FormManager.php#L258
ATT&CKT1190 T1078
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate site admin bulk-importing many Bazar forms via the UI (will share a browser UA and a single authenticated session)
  • Synthetic monitoring / uptime probe configured to POST to the form endpoint
  • Internal QA / pentest team rerunning known-exploitation tests against staging
  • Migration script run by the site owner during a YesWiki version bump
  • Search-engine / crawler misbehavior submitting forms it shouldn't (rare, but cIP will resolve to crawler ASN)
Suppression filter
| where csUserName == ""  // exclude authenticated admin bulk-imports
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the offending cIP's full request stream for the window — confirm whether the POSTs come with the wiki's auth cookies set (legit admin import) or are bare (exploitation). Check scStatus distribution; an exploitation loop typically returns 200/302 consistently. 2) Contain: block the source IP at WAF/edge and snapshot the YesWiki DB. Force-rotate every account in yeswiki_users (assume the password column has been exfiltrated). Patch to >= 4.6.4 immediately. 3) Hunt: search yeswiki_nature for rows where bn_id_nature is in the 7000000-9999999 range (the PoC's arithmetic offset signature), grep yeswiki_users for sessions logged in after the exploitation window, and pivot the source IP across other internet-facing apps for parallel scanning.
let WindowMinutes = 5m;
let PostThreshold = 20;
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csMethod =~ "POST"
| where csUriQuery has "BazaR" and csUriQuery has "vue=formulaire"
| summarize Posts = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), UserAgents = make_set(csUserAgent, 5), Statuses = make_set(scStatus, 5), Stems = make_set(csUriStem, 3)
          by cIP, sSiteName, bin(TimeGenerated, WindowMinutes)
| where Posts >= PostThreshold
| order by LastSeen desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method="POST" Web.url="*BazaR*vue=formulaire*" by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.http_user_agent, _time span=5m | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where count >= 20 | sort 0 - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method="POST" Web.url="*BazaR*vue=formulaire*" by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.http_user_agent, _time span=5m | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where count >= 20 | sort 0 - count
Non-browser User-Agent against YesWiki Bazar form-import endpoint — CVE-2026-46670 exploit tooling AIExploitation High
Hunts the PoC's exploit fingerprint: a request to /?BazaR&vue=formulaire from a scripting-language User-Agent (the published PoC uses Python-urllib/3.13). Real users post Bazar forms from a browser; a curl/python/PowerShell UA on this exact endpoint is high-signal for CVE-2026-46670 exploitation or reconnaissance. Rationale: The published PoC literally ships with User-Agent: Python-urllib/3.13 (from the Burp capture in the article body). The Bazar form-import endpoint is a low-traffic admin path on YesWiki; a scripting-language UA hitting it via POST is rarely benign and matches both the public PoC and copycat exploitation. Cross-checked against the GHSA advisory at github.com/advisories/GHSA-jwvv-qr7q-cv8j. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-jwvv-qr7q-cv8j
ATT&CKT1190 T1595.002
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate API-driven import tooling the site owner wrote (will originate from the wiki's own admin IP range)
  • curl/wget-based uptime monitoring that mistakenly probes the form-import endpoint
  • Yeswiki-admin CLI scripts that POST forms during migrations
  • Authorized vulnerability scanner (Nessus / Burp) running an authenticated assessment
  • DevOps CI job seeding test forms after a deploy
Suppression filter
| where cIP !in ("10.0.0.0/8","192.168.0.0/16","172.16.0.0/12")  // suppress internal admin/CI tooling; tune to your wiki's known-admin egress
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the source IP's recent activity — is it scanning broadly across other endpoints (mass scanner) or laser-focused on /?BazaR&vue=formulaire (targeted exploitation)? Check scStatus: 200 with growing csBytes return on each POST suggests blind data exfiltration is succeeding. 2) Contain: block the source IP at WAF/edge, then verify YesWiki version. If < 4.6.4, take the site offline pending patch and snapshot the DB. Treat yeswiki_users.password as exposed and force a global password reset. 3) Hunt: look back 30 days for any other source IPs hitting the same URI with non-browser UAs (the PoC is now public; expect copycats), and sweep all internet-facing YesWiki deployments in the estate for version <= 4.6.3.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csMethod =~ "POST"
| where csUriQuery has "BazaR" and csUriQuery has "vue=formulaire"
| where csUserAgent has_any ("Python-urllib","python-requests","curl/","Go-http-client","Java/","PowerShell","wget","libwww-perl")
| summarize Hits = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Statuses = make_set(scStatus, 5) by cIP, sSiteName, csUserAgent, csUriStem
| order by LastSeen desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Screening Serpens recruitment lure — Hiring Portal.zip + job requisition PDFs · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Tracking Iranian APT Screening Serpens’ 2026 Espionage Campaigns

Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] MiniUpdate UpdateChecker.dll sideload via legitimate signed .NET host · [LLM] Screening Serpens AppDomainManager hijack via .NET app .config tampering · Suspicious browser extension installation · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Screening Serpens C2 — DNS/network to UNC1549 infrastructure (Feb-Apr 2026) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
MiniUpdate UpdateChecker.dll sideload via legitimate signed .NET host AIInstallation High
Detects loading of the Screening Serpens MiniUpdate payload (internal name UpdateChecker.dll) by a legitimate signed .NET host process via DLL sideloading. The DLL is dropped alongside a hijack-vulnerable benign binary from the Hiring Portal.zip lure and loaded from non-standard user-writable directories. Rationale: Pivots on Unit 42's named internal DLL `UpdateChecker.dll` plus the eight published SHA256 hashes for the MiniUpdate RAT family. User-writable path filter mirrors Screening Serpens' Hiring Portal.zip ZIP-extract sideload chain. Cross-checked against Check Point's 2025 UNC1549 report and MITRE T1574.014 (AppDomainManager Injection). Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1019/ • https://research.checkpoint.com/2025/iranian-cyber-actors-target-europe/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1574/014/
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1574.014
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate vendor auto-update DLLs coincidentally named UpdateChecker.dll (e.g. Logitech, third-party LOB apps) writing to %ProgramData%
  • Internal developer build artifacts where a DLL is named UpdateChecker.dll in a project workspace under \Users\<dev>\source\
  • Endpoint security agent update DLLs unpacked to a user temp directory
  • Chocolatey / Squirrel-based app installers staging update DLLs in AppData\Local
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName !in~ ("Microsoft Corporation","Logitech","Adobe Systems Incorporated","VMware, Inc.") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files (x86)"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the loading process from DeviceImageLoadEvents/InitiatingProcessFileName — confirm whether it is a legitimate signed .NET binary residing in a user-writable path alongside an unsigned UpdateChecker.dll and a .config file (AppDomainManager hijack pattern). Verify SHA256 against the published Unit 42 IOC list and VirusTotal. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the device in Defender/MDE, kill the host process, quarantine UpdateChecker.dll and the paired host EXE+config. Reset the user's AAD/M365 credentials and revoke active sessions — Screening Serpens targets technical staff for follow-on access. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the host process hash and command line across DeviceProcessEvents for the last 30 days. Search EmailEvents for Hiring Portal.zip / Senior Software Engineer*.pdf attachments and recruitment-themed lures to the affected user. Query DNS to the four published C2 domains.

Screening Serpens AppDomainManager hijack via .NET app .config tampering AIInstallation High
Detects writes of a .NET application configuration file (appname.exe.config) containing an `appDomainManagerAssembly` / `appDomainManagerType` entry that redirects CLR initialization to a sideloaded assembly. This is the core Screening Serpens 2026 evolution that disables target app security and loads MiniUpdate/MiniJunk V2 RATs. Rationale: Targets the specific Unit 42-described evolution: AppDomainManager hijacking that manipulates .NET initialization via a legitimate .config file. The pattern of a same-directory triple (legitimate signed EXE + attacker EXE.config + attacker DLL) in user-writable paths is highly specific to this campaign and rarely seen in legitimate software, which always installs to Program Files via MSI/trusted installers. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1574/014/ • https://pentestlab.blog/2020/05/20/persistence-appdomainmanager/ • https://research.checkpoint.com/2025/iranian-cyber-actors-target-europe/
ATT&CKT1574.014 T1574.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer workstations where Visual Studio publishes a debug build to %USERPROFILE%\source\repos\<proj>\bin\ with associated app.config
  • Portable apps extracted to %APPDATA% that legitimately ship a .NET host + .config + DLLs (e.g. ShareX, Greenshot)
  • Internal LOB ClickOnce deployments dropping config+DLL pairs to %LOCALAPPDATA%\Apps
  • User-mode update agents staging new EXE+config bundles in %TEMP% before promoting them
Suppression filter
| where ConfigPath !startswith @"C:\Users\" or (ConfigPath !contains @"\source\repos\" and ConfigPath !contains @"\bin\Debug\" and ConfigPath !contains @"\bin\Release\" and ConfigPath !contains @"\AppData\Local\Apps\")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Inspect the written .exe.config file content for `<appDomainManagerAssembly>` and `<appDomainManagerType>` tags — legitimate app configs almost never set these. Verify the paired DLL is unsigned or signed by an unknown/suspicious publisher. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host in MDE. Quarantine the .config, the sideloaded DLL, and the legitimate host EXE (which would otherwise be re-triggered each launch). Disable the user's account and revoke tokens. Step 3 (hunt): Across the fleet, hunt for any other matching triples (signed .NET EXE + .config with appDomainManagerAssembly + unsigned DLL) in user-writable paths. Pull DNS for the four Screening Serpens C2 domains and any newly-created Azure-hosted *.cloudapp.azure.com / *.azurewebsites.net domains that received traffic from this host.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName endswith ".exe.config"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Users\", @"\AppData\", @"\Temp\", @"\Downloads\", @"\ProgramData\")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msiexec.exe","TrustedInstaller.exe","wusa.exe","setup.exe","installer.exe","OfficeClickToRun.exe","GoogleUpdate.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files"
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files (x86)"
| join kind=inner (
    DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where FileName endswith ".dll"
    | where FolderPath has_any (@"\Users\", @"\AppData\", @"\Temp\", @"\Downloads\", @"\ProgramData\")
    | project DllTime=Timestamp, DeviceId, DllFolder=FolderPath, DllName=FileName, DllSHA256=SHA256, DllWriter=InitiatingProcessFileName
) on DeviceId
| where abs(datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, DllTime)) < 300 and tolower(FolderPath) == tolower(DllFolder)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ConfigPath=FolderPath, ConfigName=FileName, DllName, DllSHA256, DllWriter, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let configWrites = ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName endswith ".exe.config"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Users\", @"\AppData\", @"\Temp\", @"\Downloads\", @"\ProgramData\")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("msiexec.exe","TrustedInstaller.exe","wusa.exe","setup.exe","OfficeClickToRun.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ConfigPath=TargetFilePath, ConfigName=TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine;
let dllWrites = ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName endswith ".dll"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Users\", @"\AppData\", @"\Temp\", @"\Downloads\", @"\ProgramData\")
| project DllTime=TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DllPath=TargetFilePath, DllName=TargetFileName, DllSHA256=TargetFileSHA256;
configWrites
| join kind=inner dllWrites on DvcHostname
| where abs(datetime_diff('second', TimeGenerated, DllTime)) < 300
| extend ConfigDir = substring(ConfigPath, 0, strlen(ConfigPath) - strlen(ConfigName))
| extend DllDir = substring(DllPath, 0, strlen(DllPath) - strlen(DllName))
| where tolower(ConfigDir) == tolower(DllDir)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ConfigPath, ConfigName, DllName, DllSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 (@TargetFilename:(*.exe.config OR *.EXE.config OR *.exe.CONFIG)) (@TargetFilename:(*\\Users\\* OR *\\AppData\\* OR *\\Temp\\* OR *\\Downloads\\* OR *\\ProgramData\\*)) -@Image:(*\\msiexec.exe OR *\\MsiExec.exe OR *\\TrustedInstaller.exe OR *\\OfficeClickToRun.exe)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/\.exe\.config$/i
| TargetFileName=/\\(Users|AppData|Temp|Downloads|ProgramData)\\/i
| NOT ContextImageFileName=/\\(msiexec|TrustedInstaller|OfficeClickToRun|GoogleUpdate|wusa|setup)\.exe$/i
| join({#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/\.dll$/i | TargetFileName=/\\(Users|AppData|Temp|Downloads|ProgramData)\\/i}, field=aid, key=DllAid, include=[TargetFileName, SHA256HashData, _time])
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())

Screening Serpens C2 — DNS/network to UNC1549 infrastructure (Feb-Apr 2026) AICommand & Control High
Detects any DNS resolution or network connection to the four Unit 42-published Screening Serpens C2 domains used during the Feb-Apr 2026 espionage campaign against US, Israel, UAE and Middle Eastern targets. These domains are dedicated per-target/per-variant and seeing any single resolution is high-fidelity. Rationale: All four domains are explicitly named in the Unit 42 article as Screening Serpens C2 infrastructure for the Feb-Apr 2026 MiniUpdate/MiniJunk V2 campaign. The note `buisness-centeral-transportation.com` (deliberate typosquat of `business-central-transportation`) and `ramiltonsfinance.com` are highly unusual lures unlikely to appear in benign traffic. Cross-checked against MITRE G1019 (UNC1549) and Check Point's earlier Western Europe expansion report. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1019/ • https://research.checkpoint.com/2025/iranian-cyber-actors-target-europe/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004 T1583.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researchers / threat-intel analysts performing manual lookups of the published IOCs from analyst workstations
  • Sandbox / detonation systems resolving the domains during automated triage
  • Threat-intel platforms (MISP, OpenCTI, TIP) auto-enriching indicators with active DNS lookups
  • DNS sinkholing infrastructure that proactively resolves known-bad domains for telemetry
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msedge.exe","chrome.exe","firefox.exe","iexplore.exe") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("--headless","--no-sandbox","sandbox","cuckoo","anyrun")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the host and the InitiatingProcessFileName making the resolution/connection. If the process is a browser launched by an analyst, validate against ticket/case context. If it is a non-browser process (especially a .NET host with a sideloaded DLL), treat as confirmed Screening Serpens compromise. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host in MDE/Falcon. Block the four C2 domains at the secure web gateway and DNS firewall fleet-wide. Reset and force MFA re-enrollment for the user. Step 3 (hunt): Run the MiniUpdate sideload UC and AppDomainManager hijack UC against the same host. Search EmailEvents for Hiring Portal.zip and the six job-requisition PDFs (JR205894 pattern). Look for additional Azure-hosted (cloudapp.azure.com / azurewebsites.net) domains contacted by the same process — Unit 42 notes 3-5 unique Azure-hosted domains per target.
let c2Domains = dynamic(["business-startup.org","buisness-centeral-transportation.com","premierhealthadvisory.com","ramiltonsfinance.com"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(90d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any (c2Domains) or RemoteUrl endswith ".business-startup.org" or RemoteUrl endswith ".buisness-centeral-transportation.com" or RemoteUrl endswith ".premierhealthadvisory.com" or RemoteUrl endswith ".ramiltonsfinance.com"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
let c2Domains = dynamic(["business-startup.org","buisness-centeral-transportation.com","premierhealthadvisory.com","ramiltonsfinance.com"]);
union isfuzzy=true
(DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
| where Name has_any (c2Domains)
| project TimeGenerated, Source="DnsEvents", Host=Computer, SrcIp=ClientIP, Query=Name, RemoteIp=tostring(IPAddresses)),
(ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
| where DnsQuery has_any (c2Domains)
| project TimeGenerated, Source="ImDnsActivity", Host=SrcHostname, SrcIp=SrcIpAddr, Query=DnsQuery, RemoteIp=tostring(DnsResponseName)),
(CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
| where DestinationHostName has_any (c2Domains) or DestinationDnsDomain has_any (c2Domains) or RequestURL has_any (c2Domains)
| project TimeGenerated, Source="CommonSecurityLog", Host=SourceHostName, SrcIp=SourceIP, Query=coalesce(DestinationHostName, DestinationDnsDomain, RequestURL), RemoteIp=DestinationIP),
(ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
| where Url has_any (c2Domains) or HttpHostName has_any (c2Domains)
| project TimeGenerated, Source="ImWebSession", Host=SrcHostname, SrcIp=SrcIpAddr, Query=coalesce(HttpHostName, Url), RemoteIp=DstIpAddr)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Screening Serpens recruitment lure — Hiring Portal.zip + job requisition PDFs AIDelivery High
Detects delivery of the Screening Serpens spear-phishing lure: an archive named Hiring Portal.zip (or nested within an outer ZIP) accompanied by job-requisition PDFs following the pattern '*Software Engineer*Job ID JR######*.pdf'. Targets technical personnel in aerospace, defense and telecom sectors. Rationale: Pivots on the specific lure filename `Hiring Portal.zip` named by Unit 42 (and previously by Check Point research as a Screening Serpens artifact), plus the documented job-requisition PDF pattern (e.g., `Senior Software Engineer Job ID JR205894.pdf`). Restricting to user-download locations cuts the FP rate from generic HR keyword matches on email gateways. Cross-checked against: • https://research.checkpoint.com/2025/iranian-cyber-actors-target-europe/ • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1019/
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002 T1036.005
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate HR / recruitment workflow where corporate Workday/Greenhouse exports include 'Job ID JR######' in filenames for internal hiring managers
  • Job-seeker employees saving genuine recruiter outreach attachments named 'Hiring Portal' from real airlines/aerospace firms
  • Recruiting agencies sending bulk job-spec PDFs to engineering staff (sales pipeline noise)
  • Internal mobility programs auto-emailing job requisition PDFs from the ATS
Suppression filter
| where SenderFromDomain !in~ ("workday.com","greenhouse.io","lever.co","taleo.net","icims.com","smartrecruiters.com","linkedin.com") and SenderFromDomain !endswith "@<your-corp-domain>"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Examine the sender domain and infrastructure — confirm whether the email originates from a typosquat / lookalike domain impersonating a global air carrier or major aerospace firm (Unit 42 notes the March campaign impersonated a global air carrier). Detonate Hiring Portal.zip in a sandbox; look for the nested second Hiring Portal.zip and the six job-spec PDFs. Step 2 (contain): Soft-delete the email from all recipient mailboxes via Defender for Office 365. If the user already extracted the ZIP, isolate the device and quarantine the inner archive and any extracted EXE/DLL/.config triples. Step 3 (hunt): Pull DeviceImageLoadEvents for UpdateChecker.dll and DeviceFileEvents for *.exe.config writes on the recipient's host. Run the C2 domain hunt across the fleet. Search EmailEvents for the same sender across the org — Screening Serpens runs concurrent same-day campaigns against multiple targets in a region.
let lureFileNames = dynamic(["Hiring Portal.zip","Hiring_Portal.zip","HiringPortal.zip"]);
let email = EmailAttachmentInfo
| where Timestamp > ago(60d)
| where FileName in~ (lureFileNames) or FileName matches regex @"(?i)^.*Software Engineer.*Job ID JR\d{6}.*\.pdf$" or FileName matches regex @"(?i)^.*Senior.*Engineer.*Job ID JR\d{6}.*\.pdf$"
| join kind=leftouter (EmailEvents | project NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation) on NetworkMessageId
| project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, FileName, FileType, SHA256, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation;
let host = DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(60d)
| where (FileName in~ (lureFileNames)) or (FileName matches regex @"(?i)^.*(Software|Senior|Principal).*Engineer.*Job ID JR\d{6}.*\.pdf$")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\Desktop\", @"\Temp\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, FileOriginUrl;
union email, host
| order by Timestamp desc
let lureFileNames = dynamic(["Hiring Portal.zip","Hiring_Portal.zip","HiringPortal.zip"]);
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(60d)
| where TargetFileName in~ (lureFileNames) or TargetFileName matches regex @"(?i)^.*(Software|Senior|Principal).*Engineer.*Job ID JR\d{6}.*\.pdf$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\Desktop\", @"\Temp\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time

| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

Classic macro/exploit pattern — Office app launching cmd/powershell/wmic/regsvr32.

| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
