let BadHashes = dynamic(["44f4f7aca7f1d9bfdaf7b3736934cbe19f851a707662f8f0b0c49b383e054250", "332ba2f0297dfb1599adecc3e9067893e7cf243aa23aedce4906a4c480574c17", "0db36a04d304ad96f9e6f97b531934594cd95a5cea9ff2c9af249201089dc864", "38bd137c672bd58d08c4f0502f993a6561e2c3411773d1ae57ee0151a0a9d11d", "d4a7e9f107fe40c1a5d0139c6c6e25bf6bf57f61feff090bee28f476bb3cc3c2", "bc3b44154518c5794ce639108e7b9c5fecb0c189607a26de1aaed518d890c7ad", "74882085db2088356ed7f72f01e0404a0a98cda88ef56fb15ce74c1f36b26d27", "9cf029daca89523d917dafed0568d11d00e45ec96b5b90b4a1f7fd4018c7da84", "b19e06da580cf91691eda066ac9ee4b09c6e5dc26c367af12660fe1f9306eec4", "8808c794c24367438f183e4be941876f1d3ecd0c8d2eb43b10d2380841d2283b", "43dc62cef52ebdd69e79f10015b3e13890f26c058325c0ff139c70f8d8eadcfa", "9e4a658e6d831c9e9bdfe11884a75b7c64812ed0a80e8495ddf6b316505acac1"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Paved With Intent: ROADtools and Nation-State Tactics in the Cloud

Unit 42 (Palo Alto)
2026-05-22 11 use cases 6 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Open-source framework ROADtools is being misused by threat actors for cloud intrusions. Learn how to identify its malicious use. The post Paved With Intent: ROADtools and Nation-State Tactics in the Cloud appeared first on Unit 42 .

ATT&CKT1087 T1098.005 T1190 T1528 T1550 T1566

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] UTA0355 device-code phishing: deviceCode auth flow with cross-IP token redemption · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Curious Serpens / APT29 ROADtools-pattern: device registration immediately following non-interactive token acquisition · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] ROADtools roadtx FOCI client-ID swap: refresh-token resource hop across MS Office FOCI app IDs
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Curious Serpens / APT29 ROADtools-pattern: device registration immediately following non-interactive token acquisition AIInstallation Medium
Hunts for the ROADtools roadtx device-registration sequence where an Entra ID device is registered (T1098.005) shortly after a non-interactive token grant — the pattern Microsoft attributed to Midnight Blizzard / Curious Serpens. Catches attacker-controlled devices being joined as a persistence foothold after token theft. Rationale: Article ties Cloaked Ursa/APT29 and Curious Serpens to ROADtools device-registration persistence (T1098.005). The roadtx module registers devices using one of the public FOCI client IDs (Azure CLI 04b07795, Azure PowerShell 1b730954, Microsoft Office d3590ed6) via non-interactive token flows — joining that to the Audit-Log device add within 30 minutes from a different IP catches the attacker-device persistence pattern. Cross-checked Microsoft Threat Intel reporting on Midnight Blizzard ROADtools usage. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2022/08/24/magicweb-nobeliums-post-compromise-trick-to-authenticate-as-anyone/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1098/005/ • https://www.volexity.com/blog/2025/04/22/phishing-for-codes-russian-threat-actors-target-microsoft-365-oauth-workflows/
ATT&CKT1098.005 T1550
Data sourcesAuthentication Change
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Employee enrolling a new corporate laptop while still authenticated from their old machine over VPN
  • Intune autopilot device join initiated by an IT admin from a different jump-host IP than the end-user's
  • BYOD onboarding where the user authenticates from home and the device check-in occurs over the corporate proxy
  • Conditional Access remediation flows that re-register a device after a compliance reset
  • Test-tenant red-team exercises that legitimately use ROADtools
Suppression filter
| where not(UserAgent has_any ("Microsoft-Windows-AzureAd", "MSAL.NetCore", "Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Microsoft Windows 10.0")) | where not(ClientAppUsed == "Mobile Apps and Desktop clients" and OperationName == "Add device" and ActorIp startswith "10.")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the AAD device object (Get-MgDevice) for the newly-registered device — check displayName, operatingSystem, trustType, and registeredOwners. Pivot on the actor UPN's last 24h SigninLogs to confirm geographic / ASN consistency. 2) Contain: in Entra ID admin center disable the device, revoke all sessions for the user (Revoke-MgUserSignInSession), force password reset, and require MFA re-registration. 3) Hunt: query CloudAppEvents and OfficeActivity for the actor UPN in the 24h window post-registration looking for MailItemsAccessed, FileDownloaded, eDiscovery searches, or new app-consent grants. Pivot the offending IP against AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs for other UPNs hit by the same source.
let DeviceReg = AuditLogs | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d) | where OperationName has_any ("Add registered owner to device", "Add registered users to device", "Add device") | extend TargetUpn = tostring(TargetResources[0].userPrincipalName) | extend ActorUpn = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName) | extend ActorIp = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.ipAddress) | project RegTime = TimeGenerated, ActorUpn, ActorIp, OperationName, TargetResources; let TokenAuth = AADSignInEventsBeta | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | where IsInteractive == false | where ResourceDisplayName in ("Microsoft Graph", "Azure Active Directory Graph", "Windows Azure Active Directory") | where ApplicationId in ("1b730954-1685-4b74-9bfd-dac224a7b894", "d3590ed6-52b3-4102-aeff-aad2292ab01c", "04b07795-8ddb-461a-bbee-02f9e1bf7b46") | project AuthTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, UserAgent, ApplicationId, ClientAppUsed; DeviceReg | join kind=inner TokenAuth on $left.ActorUpn == $right.AccountUpn | where datetime_diff('minute', RegTime, AuthTime) between (0 .. 30) | where ActorIp != IPAddress | project RegTime, AuthTime, MinutesBetween = datetime_diff('minute', RegTime, AuthTime), ActorUpn, RegIp = ActorIp, TokenIp = IPAddress, UserAgent, ApplicationId, ClientAppUsed
let DeviceReg = AuditLogs | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d) | where OperationName has_any ("Add registered owner to device", "Add registered users to device", "Add device") | extend ActorUpn = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName) | extend ActorIp = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.ipAddress) | project RegTime = TimeGenerated, ActorUpn, ActorIp, OperationName, TargetResources; let TokenAuth = SigninLogs | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d) | where IsInteractive == false | where ResourceDisplayName in ("Microsoft Graph", "Azure Active Directory Graph", "Windows Azure Active Directory") | where AppId in ("1b730954-1685-4b74-9bfd-dac224a7b894", "d3590ed6-52b3-4102-aeff-aad2292ab01c", "04b07795-8ddb-461a-bbee-02f9e1bf7b46") | project AuthTime = TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, UserAgent, AppId, AppDisplayName, ClientAppUsed; DeviceReg | join kind=inner TokenAuth on $left.ActorUpn == $right.UserPrincipalName | where datetime_diff('minute', RegTime, AuthTime) between (0 .. 30) | where ActorIp != IPAddress | project RegTime, AuthTime, MinutesBetween = datetime_diff('minute', RegTime, AuthTime), ActorUpn, RegIp = ActorIp, TokenIp = IPAddress, UserAgent, AppId, AppDisplayName, ClientAppUsed

UTA0355 device-code phishing: deviceCode auth flow with cross-IP token redemption AIDelivery High
Hunts for the UTA0355 (Volexity, 2025) targeted phishing TTP where a victim is sent a device-code prompt and the resulting token is redeemed from attacker infrastructure. ROADtools' roadtx module supports the device_code flow natively; the cross-IP redemption (different IP between code issuance and token use) is the high-fidelity signal. Rationale: Article explicitly cites Volexity's UTA0355 device-code phishing campaign and notes roadtx's device_code flow support. Device-code authentication is rare in normal user populations and a multi-IP redemption inside a 15-minute window is a near-textbook indicator of phished-code abuse — Volexity called this exact pattern out as the UTA0355 IoC. Cross-checked Volexity's April 2025 report. Cross-checked against: • https://www.volexity.com/blog/2025/04/22/phishing-for-codes-russian-threat-actors-target-microsoft-365-oauth-workflows/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1528/ • https://github.com/dirkjanm/ROADtools
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1528 T1550.001
Data sourcesAuthentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Conference-room shared device sign-in where a user types a code from their phone (legitimate device-code flow, but typically same network)
  • IT admin demoing device-code flow during training
  • Smart-TV / Apple-TV style sign-in to corporate streaming apps
  • User on mobile network completing device-code on laptop simultaneously (legit cross-IP, same person)
  • Penetration test or purple-team exercise
Suppression filter
| where not(SrcCountries has_any (dynamic(["US","US"])) and array_length(SrcCountries) == 1) | where not(UAs has "Microsoft.WindowsAzureMediaServices")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the SigninLogs records for the UPN, examine AuthenticationDetails and CorrelationId. Confirm the device-code issuance IP vs redemption IP — geo, ASN, ISP. Check the user's mailbox for an inbound message containing https://microsoft.com/devicelogin or a Teams chat with that URL in the 30 minutes before code issuance. 2) Contain: Revoke-MgUserSignInSession for the UPN, disable all refresh tokens, force interactive MFA re-auth, block the redemption IP at the Conditional Access named-location level. 3) Hunt: pivot the redemption IP across SigninLogs for other UPNs; check AuditLogs for device-add, app-consent, or mailbox-rule events under that UPN in the next 6 hours.

ROADtools roadtx FOCI client-ID swap: refresh-token resource hop across MS Office FOCI app IDs AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts for roadtx's signature behaviour of exchanging a refresh token issued to one Microsoft Family of Client IDs (FOCI) app for an access token on a different FOCI app — a defense-evasion trick to broaden token scope without re-prompting MFA. Detection identifies the same refresh-token correlation hitting multiple FOCI app IDs within a short window. Rationale: Article describes roadtx exploiting OAuth on-behalf-of and refresh-token reuse to enable persistence and broaden access; this matches the publicly-documented FOCI refresh-token hopping behaviour (Secureworks, Microsoft research). Detecting >=3 distinct FOCI client IDs sharing refresh-token continuity in <10 minutes for one UPN is high-fidelity for roadtx token replay. Cross-checked Secureworks FOCI research and dirkjanm/ROADtools GitHub. Cross-checked against: • https://www.secureworks.com/research/family-of-client-ids • https://github.com/dirkjanm/ROADtools • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1550/001/
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1606.002
Data sourcesAuthentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A user on Windows logging into Outlook, OneDrive, Teams, and Edge in quick succession after a fresh sign-in (legit FOCI SSO)
  • IT pilot of new Microsoft 365 app rollouts where users authenticate to many M365 endpoints in sequence
  • Mobile-device enrollment flows where Authenticator App, Intune Company Portal, and Office hit Graph back-to-back
  • Browser-based passwordless flow where Edge proxies tokens to several MS apps
  • Service-account driven automation that exercises multiple Graph scopes
Suppression filter
| where not(UAs has_any ("Microsoft.WindowsAzureMediaServices", "Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Microsoft Windows 10.0", "Microsoft Office", "OneDrive")) | where not(array_length(SrcIPs) == 1 and SrcIPs has_any (dynamic(["10.","172.16.","192.168."])))
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the burst's SrcIPs and UserAgents — single-IP non-Microsoft UA strings (curl, python-requests, MSAL Python) on a desktop UPN is highly suspicious. Pull CorrelationId and trace the parent token chain in SigninLogs. 2) Contain: Revoke-MgUserSignInSession, invalidate refresh tokens, and apply a Conditional Access policy requiring compliant-device for the offending UPN. 3) Hunt: pivot UserAgent and IPAddress across SigninLogs for other UPNs exhibiting the same multi-FOCI burst; check AuditLogs for application-consent grants, new service-principal credentials, and Exchange mailbox-rule additions in the 24h window.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] PowerShell-parented taskkill of winrar.exe (Cloud Atlas LNK anti-forensic cleanup) · [LLM] PowerShower dropped to user Pictures folder as googleearth.ps1 · [LLM] termsrv.dll patched (multi-RDP enabling) - takeown + binary write + TermService restart · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] OpenSSH reverse port-forward (-R) launched on a workstation - Cloud Atlas backup C2 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] SAM/SECURITY registry hives copied from VSS shadow to Public\Documents as .pdf · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
PowerShell-parented taskkill of winrar.exe (Cloud Atlas LNK anti-forensic cleanup) AIInstallation High
Hunts the Step 6 'process concealment' action in the Fixed.ps1 loader chain - PowerShell spawning taskkill.exe /F /IM winrar.exe immediately after the LNK-launched stager extracts the decoy PDF. This pairing is highly article-specific and uncommon outside attacker cleanup routines. Rationale: Anchored on the exact Step 6 string from the article's Fixed.ps1 action table: 'taskkill.exe /F /Im winrar.exe' with PowerShell as parent. Cross-checked Cloud Atlas (aka Inception) on MITRE ATT&CK G0100 confirms loader pattern. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0100/ • https://securelist.com/cloud-atlas/68083/
ATT&CKT1070.004 T1562.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT helpdesk scripts that close hung WinRAR instances via PowerShell remote sessions
  • Endpoint management tools (PDQ Deploy/SCCM) running PowerShell cleanup that kills GUI archivers before silent install
  • Developer build scripts wrapping 7z/WinRAR and force-terminating the GUI on failure
  • Forensic-acquisition scripts that ensure WinRAR isn't holding evidence file handles
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("PDQDeployRunner.exe", "ccmexec.exe", "MsMpEng.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Windows\\CCM"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !contains "PDQ"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the PowerShell parent's full command line and InitiatingProcessParentFileName - confirm it traces back to an LNK launch from %TEMP% or a user-downloaded ZIP and not from svc/sysadmin context. Inspect the host for $temp\fixed.ps1, $temp\rar.zip, and *.pdf.lnk artefacts. 2) Contain: isolate the host via Defender Live Response or EDR network containment; collect $temp, %APPDATA%, and the user's Pictures folder (PowerShower drop path) before reboot. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same AccountName for HKCU\...\Run\YandexBrowser_setup registry creation, googleearth.ps1 in Pictures, and outbound traffic to the article IOC IPs (194.102.104.207, 46.17.45.x, 185.22.154.73).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "taskkill.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "winrar.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/F", "/IM")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "powershell.exe"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\taskkill.exe"
| where CommandLine contains "winrar.exe"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\powershell.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
title: PowerShell spawning taskkill against winrar.exe (Cloud Atlas anti-forensic)
id: 8a3e3c9c-1d5f-4d1a-9e9b-1c0c8c4a7e11
description: Detects PowerShell parent process spawning taskkill.exe targeting winrar.exe - Cloud Atlas Fixed.ps1 loader cleanup step 6.
references:
  - https://securelist.com/cloud-atlas-2026/119895/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/23
tags:
  - attack.t1070.004
  - attack.t1562.001
  - attack.defense_evasion
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_img:
    Image|endswith: '\taskkill.exe'
    ParentImage|endswith: '\powershell.exe'
  selection_cmd:
    CommandLine|contains: 'winrar.exe'
  selection_flags:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '/F'
      - '/IM'
  condition: selection_img and selection_cmd and selection_flags
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\taskkill.exe OR *\\TASKKILL.EXE) @CommandLine:(*winrar.exe* OR *WinRAR.exe* OR *WINRAR.EXE*) @ParentImage:(*\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\POWERSHELL.EXE)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\taskkill\.exe$/i ParentBaseFileName=/powershell\.exe$/i
| regex("(?i)winrar\\.exe", field=CommandLine)
| regex("(?i)\\s/(F|IM)\\s", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=taskkill.exe Processes.process="*winrar.exe*" Processes.parent_process_name=powershell.exe by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where match(process, "(?i)/F") OR match(process, "(?i)/IM") | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`

PowerShower dropped to user Pictures folder as googleearth.ps1 AIInstallation High
Hunts the documented PowerShower install path 'C:\Users\[username]\Pictures\googleearth.ps1' - an unusual location/name combination Cloud Atlas uses to hide its reconnaissance/Kerberoasting backdoor. Catches both the file-drop event and subsequent PowerShell execution. Rationale: Direct quote from article: 'PowerShower is dropped onto the system via the path C:\Users\[username]\Pictures\googleearth.ps1.' Filename + path combo is uniquely Cloud Atlas - Google Earth doesn't ship a .ps1 and Pictures isn't a normal script location. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0441/ • https://malpedia.caad.fkie.fraunhofer.de/details/win.powershower
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1547.001 T1564.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User legitimately syncing a script named googleearth.ps1 via OneDrive/Dropbox into their Pictures folder (rare)
  • Photography or GIS hobbyist scripting Google Earth automation and naming files in Pictures
  • Internal red-team exercise emulating Cloud Atlas using the same IOC paths
  • Backup software previewing/restoring a previously-infected file
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files\\Google\\"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("OneDrive.exe", "Dropbox.exe", "GoogleDriveFS.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash the dropped googleearth.ps1 (MD5 against article IOC list 5329f7bff9d0d5db28821b86c26d628f, 7a95360b7e0eb5b107a3d231abbc541a, c0d1eaa15a2cefbab9735787575c8d8e, d5b38b252cf212a4a32763de36732d40, 3c75cedb1196df5eab91f31411ed4b33, 42ac350bfbc5b4eb0fedba16c81919c7, 493b901d1b33eb577db64aadd948f9ce). Confirm the script contains PowerShower indicators (process enumeration, AD admin group queries, Kerberoasting). 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the parent PowerShell, delete the .ps1, and remove HKCU\...\Run\YandexBrowser_setup. Reset any AD account that logged on during the dwell window. 3) Hunt: cross-org search for googleearth.ps1 in Pictures, Kerberoast SPN-request bursts from the same account (4769 with RC4 ticket encryption), and outbound to article C2 (tenkoff.org, cloudguide.in, goverru.com, kufar.org, ultimatecore.net, onedrivesupport.net).
union
(DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
  | where ProcessCommandLine has "googleearth.ps1"
  | where ProcessCommandLine has @"\Pictures\" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has @"\Pictures\"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, EventKind="Process", FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine),
(DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
  | where FileName =~ "googleearth.ps1"
  | where FolderPath has @"\Pictures\"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, EventKind="FileDrop", FileName, ProcessCommandLine=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine)
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine contains "googleearth.ps1"
| where CommandLine contains "Pictures"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName

SAM/SECURITY registry hives copied from VSS shadow to Public\Documents as .pdf AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the PowerShower credential grabber: a Volume Shadow Copy is created and SAM/SECURITY hives are copied to C:\Users\Public\Documents\ disguised with a .pdf extension. The combination of HarddiskVolumeShadowCopy source paths, Public\Documents destination, and .pdf masquerade is unique to this article. Rationale: Article states verbatim: 'Copies the SAM (stores local user password hashes) and SECURITY system files from this shadow copy to C:\Users\Public\Documents\, disguising them as PDF files.' The triple constraint (Public\Documents + .pdf + SAM/SECURITY/shadow-copy reference) collapses FP rate to near zero. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/002/ • https://malpedia.caad.fkie.fraunhofer.de/details/win.powershower
ATT&CKT1003.002 T1003.004 T1006 T1036.008
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Veeam/Acronis backup agents creating shadow copies and staging files in Public\Documents (won't match SAM/SECURITY filter)
  • Sysadmin running a SAM/SECURITY backup test in a documented IR engagement
  • Disaster-recovery script copying registry hives to a known location (legit, but rare path choice)
  • Security tooling (Velociraptor, KAPE) collecting hives - usually goes to %ProgramData% not Public\Documents
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("veeam.backup.shell.exe", "acrocmd.exe", "AcronisAgent.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !contains "KAPE"
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("services.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full PowerShell parent chain and look for the fodhelper.exe UAC-bypass parent (DeviceProcessEvents InitiatingProcessParentFileName == fodhelper.exe). Inspect C:\Users\Public\Documents\ for *.pdf files whose magic bytes are 'regf' (registry hive). 2) Contain: isolate the host immediately, treat ALL local accounts and the logged-on domain account as compromised, force enterprise password rotation for that user and any cached creds, revoke Kerberos TGTs (krbtgt rotation if domain controller affected). 3) Hunt: search for fodhelper.exe spawning PowerShell across the fleet, Kerberoast SPN requests from the same account, and outbound exfil to article C2 IPs/domains. Pivot on any other host in the same OU.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has @"\Users\Public\Documents\" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has @"\Users\Public\Documents\"
| where ProcessCommandLine has ".pdf" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has ".pdf"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("SAM", "SECURITY", "HarddiskVolumeShadowCopy", "Win32_ShadowCopy", "vssadmin")
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("SAM", "SECURITY", "HarddiskVolumeShadowCopy", "Win32_ShadowCopy", "vssadmin")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "cmd.exe", "wmic.exe", "fodhelper.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine contains "Public\\Documents"
| where CommandLine contains ".pdf"
| where CommandLine has_any ("SAM", "SECURITY", "HarddiskVolumeShadowCopy", "Win32_ShadowCopy", "vssadmin")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
title: SAM/SECURITY hive exfil-staged in Public Documents as PDF (Cloud Atlas PowerShower)

#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| regex("(?i)\\\\Users\\\\Public\\\\Documents\\\\", field=CommandLine)

termsrv.dll patched (multi-RDP enabling) - takeown + binary write + TermService restart AIInstallation High
Hunts Cloud Atlas's rdp_new.ps1 (MD5 1a11b26dd0261ef27a112ce8b361c247) which takes ownership of termsrv.dll, patches the 39 81 3C 06 00 00 byte sequence to B8 00 01 00 00 89 81 38 06 00 00 90 to allow concurrent RDP sessions, then restarts TermService. Lets attacker share the host invisibly with the legit user. Rationale: Anchored on the article's exact script name (rdp_new.ps1, MD5 1a11b26dd0261ef27a112ce8b361c247), the unique target file (termsrv.dll), the documented takeown+permissions+patch+restart chain, and the verbatim byte-pattern sequences in code blocks [1] and [2]. termsrv.dll modification outside of Windows Update/TrustedInstaller is exceedingly rare. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/001/ • https://github.com/stascorp/rdpwrap
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1112 T1021.001 T1547.014
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • RDPWrap installation by an admin to enable concurrent sessions on a non-server SKU (same TTP, different actor)
  • Windows feature-update where termsrv.dll is replaced by TrustedInstaller (excluded by parent filter)
  • IT engineer troubleshooting Remote Desktop Services and restarting TermService
  • Pen-test tooling that explicitly modifies termsrv.dll for ATT&CK emulation
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("TrustedInstaller.exe", "TiWorker.exe", "msiexec.exe", "wuauclt.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Windows\\WinSxS\\"
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Windows\\servicing\\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash termsrv.dll against the Microsoft-signed catalog for the OS build (sigcheck -h -c C:\Windows\System32\termsrv.dll) - any unsigned/altered hash is positive. Pull rdp_new.ps1 (MD5 1a11b26dd0261ef27a112ce8b361c247) from the host. Check fDenyTSConnections=0 and MaxInstanceCount registry changes. 2) Contain: isolate via EDR, restore termsrv.dll from a clean baseline (sfc /scannow then dism /restorehealth, or robocopy from a peer system), restart TermService, force-disconnect any active RDP sessions, reset the user and any admin accounts that logged on. 3) Hunt: search for the byte pattern '39 81 3C 06 00 00' replacement across the fleet via EDR YARA, look for ssh.exe with -R flag (reverse tunnel UC), and outbound to article IOC IPs.
let TermsrvProc = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
    | where ProcessCommandLine has "termsrv.dll"
    | where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("takeown", "icacls", "TermService", "Restart-Service", "Stop-Service", "net stop termservice", "sc ")
        or FileName in~ ("takeown.exe", "icacls.exe")
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, EventKind="Proc", FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine;
let TermsrvFileWrite = DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
    | where FolderPath endswith @"\System32" and FileName =~ "termsrv.dll"
    | where ActionType in ("FileModified", "FileCreated", "FileRenamed")
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("TrustedInstaller.exe", "msiexec.exe", "TiWorker.exe")
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, EventKind="FileWrite", FileName, ProcessCommandLine=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine;
union TermsrvProc, TermsrvFileWrite
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine contains "termsrv.dll"
| where CommandLine has_any ("takeown", "icacls", "TermService", "Restart-Service", "Stop-Service")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
title: termsrv.dll patched for multi-RDP (Cloud Atlas rdp_new.ps1)

#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2

OpenSSH reverse port-forward (-R) launched on a workstation - Cloud Atlas backup C2 AICommand & Control High
Hunts the reverse SSH tunnel installer Cloud Atlas drops via PsExec/PAExec: VBS scripts launch ssh.exe with -R to expose the victim's internal port to an attacker-controlled server. Detection focuses on ssh.exe with the -R flag on Windows endpoints where SSH client use is not part of the normal admin workflow. Rationale: Article: 'To install a reverse SSH tunnel on a victim's host, the attackers run VBS scripts via PAExec or PsExec.' The -R flag is the canonical reverse-port-forward switch; combining it with VBS/PsExec parents removes the noise from legitimate developer/admin SSH use. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1572/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1090/001/
ATT&CKT1572 T1090.001 T1219 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Network/sysadmin using ssh -R to set up jump-host access for legitimate remote management (typically from a known admin workstation, not VBS-spawned)
  • Developer running ssh -R for ngrok-like service exposure during local development
  • Cloud automation tool (Ansible, Terraform) using SSH reverse tunnels for callback (parent would be Python/Ansible, not wscript)
  • Internal Linux-on-Windows WSL workflows that invoke ssh.exe (typically interactive shell parent)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files\\Git\\"
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Users\\" or InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("code.exe", "WindowsTerminal.exe", "pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine !contains "github.com"
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the full ssh.exe command line and the -R argument target (host:port). Geo-lookup the destination - article IOC IPs are 194.102.104.207, 46.17.45.49/56, 46.17.44.125/212, 185.22.154.73, 194.87.196.163, 195.58.49.9. Pull the parent VBS script body (likely under %TEMP% or C:\Windows\Temp) and the PsExec/PAExec command line that staged it. 2) Contain: kill the ssh.exe PID, isolate the host, block the destination IP at the egress firewall, revoke any private keys present in %USERPROFILE%\.ssh\ and rotate matching authorized_keys on attacker-suspected servers. 3) Hunt: pivot on PsExec/PAExec service installations (event 7045 + service name length 1-2 chars) across the domain, search for the patched OpenSSH binary hash, and look for additional outbound :22/:443 connections to article IOC IP ranges.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName =~ "ssh.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\s-R\s+\S+"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe", "cscript.exe", "cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "psexec.exe", "psexec64.exe", "paexec.exe", "services.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| join kind=leftouter (
    DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "ssh.exe"
    | where RemotePort == 22 or RemotePort == 443
    | project NetTime=Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
  ) on DeviceName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\ssh.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\s-R\s+\S+"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("wscript.exe", "cscript.exe", "cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "PsExec.exe", "paexec.exe", "services.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName

C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.

| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2018-0802")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2018-0802")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    from datamodel=Email.All_Email

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.

    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/

    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:

            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'

    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1021.002
    - attack.t1569.002
    - attack.lateral-movement
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_psexec:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\psexec.exe'
            - '\psexec64.exe'
            - '\psexesvc.exe'
            - '\paexec.exe'
            - '\csexec.exe'
            - '\remcom.exe'
            - '\smbexec.py'
    selection_wmic_remote:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\wmic.exe'
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '/node:'
    condition: selection_psexec or selection_wmic_remote
falsepositives:
    - Sysadmins running approved remote-management tooling — wrap with
      a known-admin-host watchlist
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args Installation High
schtasks.exe /create or Microsoft-Windows-TaskScheduler EventID 4698 with LOLBin actions.
ATT&CKT1053.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/create"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("powershell","cmd.exe","rundll32","-enc","FromBase64","\Users\Public","\AppData\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\schtasks.exe"
| where CommandLine has "/create"
| where CommandLine has_any ("powershell","cmd.exe","rundll32","-enc","FromBase64",
                              "\Users\Public", "\AppData\")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName, NewProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Scheduled Task Creation with Suspicious Image / Encoded Args
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0d
status: experimental
description: |
    schtasks.exe /create with payload-shaped action — points at
    powershell, cmd, rundll32, encoded-base64, or user-writable paths.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1053/005/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1053.005
    - attack.persistence
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_schtasks:
        Image|endswith: '\schtasks.exe'
        CommandLine|contains: '/create'
    selection_payload:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'powershell'
            - 'cmd.exe'
            - 'rundll32'
            - '-enc'
            - 'FromBase64'
            - '\Users\Public'
            - '\AppData\'
    condition: selection_schtasks and selection_payload
falsepositives:
    - GPO-driven scheduled tasks, MDT/SCCM imaging
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name="schtasks.exe" AND Processes.process="*/create*"
      AND (Processes.process="*powershell*" OR Processes.process="*cmd.exe*"
        OR Processes.process="*rundll32*" OR Processes.process="*-enc*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*\Users\Public*"
        OR Processes.process="*\AppData\*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name="schtasks.exe" AND Processes.process="*/create*"
      AND (Processes.process="*powershell*" OR Processes.process="*cmd.exe*"
        OR Processes.process="*rundll32*" OR Processes.process="*-enc*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*\Users\Public*"
        OR Processes.process="*\AppData\*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
